note: Fields marked NOT_AVAILABLE indicate genuine absence of source-backed evidence. Do NOT infer or fabricate.

chilli_healthy.leaf_symptoms: No visible symptoms. Leaves are dark green, flat, and turgid with no lesions, curl, or discoloration.
chilli_healthy.visual_appearance: Uniform dark green color, intact leaf margins, no lesions or mottling.
chilli_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy leaves lack any curl, lesions, spots, or yellowing.
chilli_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Inspect weekly for early signs of leaf curl (viral) or circular spots (fungal). Scout lower canopy first.
chilli_healthy.prevention: Use certified virus-free seeds. Control thrips and aphid vectors. Apply balanced fertilization. Avoid water stress. Maintain proper spacing for airflow.
chilli_healthy.cultural_management: Remove volunteer chilli plants. Maintain field hygiene. Avoid waterlogging.
chilli_healthy.sanitation: Remove crop debris after harvest. Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops.
chilli_healthy.water_irrigation_management: Avoid overhead irrigation where possible. Maintain soil moisture without waterlogging.
chilli_healthy.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals or legumes. Avoid planting chilli after tomato, pepper, or potato (solanaceous family).
chilli_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE — consult ICAR-IIVR or state KVK for current resistant variety recommendations.
chilli_healthy.knowledge_notes: Healthy class — monitoring and prevention are primary knowledge domains.

chilli_leaf_curl.scientific_name: Chilli Leaf Curl Virus (ChiLCV) — a Begomovirus; also associated with Chilli Veinal Mottle Virus (ChiVMV)
chilli_leaf_curl.pathogen_or_cause: Begomovirus (predominantly Chilli Leaf Curl Virus, ChiLCV); transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
chilli_leaf_curl.leaf_symptoms: Marked upward or downward curling and rolling of leaves. Leaves become leathery, distorted, and wrinkled. Older leaves show crinkling with interveinal mottling. Leaf size is reduced.
chilli_leaf_curl.stem_symptoms: Shortening of internodes; stunted plant growth. Tip curl in growing shoots.
chilli_leaf_curl.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Fruits are small, distorted, and misshapen. Yield is significantly reduced.
chilli_leaf_curl.early_symptoms: Youngest leaves curl upward or inward. Mild mottling or yellowing at leaf margins.
chilli_leaf_curl.advanced_symptoms: Severe curling of most leaves. Interveinal clearing. Stunted plant. Premature leaf fall.
chilli_leaf_curl.visual_appearance: Affected leaves are curled, cupped, and chlorotic. Plant appears bushy but stunted.
chilli_leaf_curl.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Upward/downward curling combined with interveinal mottling and leaf distortion; characteristic of Begomovirus infection. Whiteflies may be visible on the lower leaf surface.
lookalike_conditions: Nutrient deficiency (zinc deficiency can cause curl)
chilli_leaf_curl.visual_differentiation: Curl virus causes distinctive puckering and interveinal mottling alongside curling. Leaf spot produces discrete circular lesions without curling.
chilli_leaf_curl.disease_cycle_summary: ChiLCV overwinters in alternate hosts. Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) acquire the virus from infected plants and transmit it to healthy chilli within minutes of feeding. The disease spreads rapidly in warm, dry conditions when whitefly populations are high.
chilli_leaf_curl.spread_mechanism: Exclusively vector-transmitted through whitefly Bemisia tabaci (persistent, circulative manner). Not mechanically transmitted or soil-borne.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (25–35°C) favor whitefly population build-up and virus spread.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: Low relative humidity (40–60%) is associated with high whitefly activity and disease spread.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Dry conditions favor whitefly multiplication. Monsoon rains reduce whitefly activity.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — no specific soil factor established for this viral disease.

chilli_leaf_curl.growth_stage_context: Most damaging at seedling and early vegetative stages. Plants infected before flowering suffer severe yield loss.
chilli_leaf_curl.monitoring_guidance: Monitor for whitefly populations weekly. Use yellow sticky traps (1 per 250 m²). Inspect growing tips and underside of young leaves. Scout field borders first as whiteflies colonize edges.
chilli_leaf_curl.prevention: Use virus-free certified seeds. Use healthy nursery transplants. Raise nursery under 50-mesh nylon net to exclude whitefly. Remove weed hosts (e.g., Solanum nigrum) from field borders. Avoid growing chilli near tomato or other solanaceous crops to reduce whitefly buildup.
chilli_leaf_curl.cultural_management: Remove and destroy heavily infected plants immediately. Intercrop with maize or sorghum rows as wind barriers to reduce whitefly movement. Reflective mulches (silver polyethylene) reduce whitefly landing.
chilli_leaf_curl.sanitation: Uproot and destroy crop debris after harvest. Remove alternate host weeds. Do not carry infected plant material between fields.
chilli_leaf_curl.water_irrigation_management: Maintain plant vigor with adequate irrigation. Avoid water stress, which can worsen susceptibility.
chilli_leaf_curl.crop_rotation: Avoid successive chilli or solanaceous crops in the same field.
chilli_leaf_curl.resistant_varieties: Some tolerant varieties exist. Consult ICAR-IIVR or state agricultural universities for current resistant variety recommendations for your region.
chilli_leaf_curl.biological_control: Encourage natural enemies of whitefly (e.g., Encarsia formosa parasitoid, Chrysoperla eggs). Release 50,000 Chrysoperla eggs/ha at early infestation stage where commercially available.
chilli_leaf_curl.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for whitefly control on chilli in your region. Systemic insecticides targeting Bemisia tabaci are commonly used in India — consult local agricultural extension or product label for current registered options and rates. Avoid overuse of any single class of insecticide to prevent resistance.
chilli_leaf_curl.expert_escalation_conditions: If more than 30–40% plants show symptoms, and whitefly control is not reducing spread, contact plant pathologist or agricultural extension officer. Entire field may need replanting with resistant variety.
chilli_leaf_curl.knowledge_notes: Predominantly managed through vector control, not fungicide. Specific chemical names excluded to avoid hallucination of rates/registration.

source_references.organization: ANGRAU (Acharya N G Ranga Agricultural University)

chilli_leaf_spot.disease_name: Chilli Leaf Spot (Cercospora Leaf Spot / Anthracnose Leaf Spot)
chilli_leaf_spot.scientific_name: Cercospora capsici (Heald & F.A. Wolf) — Cercospora leaf spot; Colletotrichum spp. can also cause fruit/leaf spots
chilli_leaf_spot.pathogen_or_cause: Cercospora capsici (primary fungal cause of Cercospora leaf spot in chilli)
chilli_leaf_spot.leaf_symptoms: Circular to irregular water-soaked lesions that turn brown with pale gray or white necrotic centers. Lesions typically have a yellow halo. Multiple lesions coalesce to form larger irregular blighted areas. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely.
chilli_leaf_spot.stem_symptoms: Stem lesions possible on petioles causing defoliation.
chilli_leaf_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: In severe cases, dark sunken lesions may appear on fruits.
chilli_leaf_spot.early_symptoms: Small water-soaked circular spots (2–5 mm) on leaf surface, initially pale green.
chilli_leaf_spot.advanced_symptoms: Spots enlarge to 1–2 cm, turn brown with gray-white centers. Mass defoliation. Lower canopy affected first.
chilli_leaf_spot.visual_appearance: Brown circular spots with pale gray centers and prominent yellow chlorotic halos on leaves. Concentric ring patterns may be visible.
chilli_leaf_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Circular lesions with gray-white powdery centers (due to fungal sporulation) and yellow halo; predominantly on lower/older leaves.
lookalike_conditions: Phytophthora leaf spot (larger, water-soaked, margin less distinct)
Chilli bacterial spot (angular lesions constrained by veins)
Chilli anthracnose (sunken spots, more on fruit)
chilli_leaf_spot.visual_differentiation: Cercospora leaf spot produces circular gray-centered lesions with yellow halos. Bacterial spot produces angular water-soaked lesions limited by leaf veins.
chilli_leaf_spot.disease_cycle_summary: Cercospora capsici survives in infected crop debris and soil. Spores (conidia) are dispersed by wind and rain splash. Infection is favored by warm, humid conditions. Multiple infection cycles can occur in one season.
chilli_leaf_spot.spread_mechanism: Wind dispersal and rain splash of fungal spores (conidia).

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Optimal temperature range 25–30°C for disease development. ICAR sources document significant infection at these warm temperatures.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity (>80%) and prolonged leaf wetness (>6 hours) facilitate spore germination and infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rainfall and overhead irrigation promote rain splash dispersal of spores. Disease is severe in humid tropical regions during wet season.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — no specific soil factor established beyond general crop hygiene.

chilli_leaf_spot.growth_stage_context: Disease most common at vegetative and flowering stages. Lower canopy leaves affected earliest due to higher humidity near ground.
chilli_leaf_spot.monitoring_guidance: Inspect lower canopy leaves weekly. Count lesion number on 10 randomly selected plants. High incidence warrants intervention. Scout after prolonged wet or humid weather.
chilli_leaf_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds. Treat seeds with hot water (52°C for 30 minutes) or recommended fungicide before planting. Space plants adequately (60 × 45 cm) for airflow. Avoid overhead irrigation.
chilli_leaf_spot.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris. Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet (to prevent mechanical spread). Use drip irrigation over overhead spray.
chilli_leaf_spot.sanitation: Deep plough and destroy crop debris after harvest. Avoid leaving infected chilli plants in field.
chilli_leaf_spot.water_irrigation_management: Use drip or furrow irrigation rather than overhead sprinkler. Irrigate in the morning to allow leaves to dry during the day.
chilli_leaf_spot.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals or legumes for at least 2 seasons to reduce soil inoculum. Avoid consecutive chilli/capsicum crops.
chilli_leaf_spot.resistant_varieties: Some tolerant varieties have been identified at ICAR-IIVR. Consult current state KVK recommendations for varieties available in your region.
chilli_leaf_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE — no commercially validated biocontrol agent for Cercospora on chilli documented in reviewed Indian sources.
chilli_leaf_spot.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for Cercospora leaf spot on chilli in your region and follow product label guidance. Copper-based fungicides and mancozeb-based products are commonly referenced in Indian extension literature; however, specific rates and intervals must follow current product labels and local extension recommendation.
chilli_leaf_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: If defoliation exceeds 40–50% or lesions appear on fruits, contact agricultural extension immediately. Repeated fungicide failure warrants resistance testing.
chilli_leaf_spot.knowledge_notes: Specific chemical rates excluded to avoid hallucination. Indian extension sources confirm warm humid conditions as primary risk factor.

corn_gray_leaf_spot.pathogen_or_cause: Cercospora zeina (predominant in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia) and Cercospora zeae-maydis
corn_gray_leaf_spot.leaf_symptoms: Rectangular to elongated gray-tan lesions bounded by leaf veins on both sides, giving a rectangular appearance unique among maize diseases. Lesions are initially tan-brown, becoming grayish-white to pale tan as they age. Lesions may coalesce to cause blighting of entire leaves.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.stem_symptoms: Leaf sheaths may also be affected with irregular tan lesions.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Husk and ear leaves may show lesions in severe cases.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.early_symptoms: Small, yellowish-tan water-soaked rectangular spots (2–4 mm wide, up to 50 mm long) on lower leaves.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.advanced_symptoms: Lesions expand lengthwise, turn pale gray, and are bounded by veins on either side. Mass leaf blighting causes early senescence. Lower leaves affected first.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.visual_appearance: Distinctive rectangular or oblong pale gray lesions aligned with leaf venation. Lesions have parallel edges due to vein restriction.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Rectangular gray lesions with parallel edges (constrained by leaf veins) are pathognomonic for Gray Leaf Spot.
lookalike_conditions: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (larger cigar-shaped elliptical lesions, not vein-constrained)
Southern Corn Leaf Blight (smaller elongated lesions)
Eyespot (smaller circular lesions with yellow halo)
corn_gray_leaf_spot.visual_differentiation: GLS lesions are strictly rectangular/vein-constrained and gray-tan. NCLB lesions are cigar-shaped, tan-brown, not constrained by veins.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.disease_cycle_summary: C. zeina survives on infected crop debris in soil. Conidia are released under high humidity and spread via wind/rain splash to lower canopy leaves. Disease progresses upward. Favorable conditions allow rapid multiplication through multiple cycles.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash of conidia from infected crop residue.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Optimal development between 25–30°C. Disease is severe in warm humid areas.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: Prolonged high relative humidity (>90%) and leaf wetness (>11 hours) are strongly associated with infection. Dew formation is critical.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rainfall and high dew periods support epidemic development. Conservation tillage that leaves crop residue is a major risk factor.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — no specific soil association documented; conservation tillage practice is the key risk factor.

corn_gray_leaf_spot.growth_stage_context: Most damaging when infection occurs before tasseling (VT/R1). Lower canopy leaves infected at vegetative stage; progresses to ear leaves affecting grain fill.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.monitoring_guidance: Scout at VT/R1 stage for lesions on lower leaf canopy. Assess percentage leaf area affected on ear leaf and two leaves above/below.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.prevention: Plant resistant/tolerant hybrids (primary management strategy). Rotate crops with non-host (soybean, wheat). Avoid conservation tillage on high-risk fields or implement residue management. Improve plant spacing and row orientation for better airflow.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.cultural_management: Bury or remove crop residue. Practice crop rotation. Plant resistant hybrids.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.sanitation: Deep ploughing to bury residue. Avoid leaving large amounts of maize debris on the soil surface.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.water_irrigation_management: Avoid excessive irrigation that creates high humidity conditions near the canopy.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-grass crops (soybean, cotton, legumes) to reduce residue-borne inoculum.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.resistant_varieties: Resistant hybrids are the most effective management approach. Consult ICAR-IIMR, state agricultural universities or seed company for current GLS-resistant maize hybrids recommended for your region.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE — no commercially established biocontrol for GLS documented in reviewed sources.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for Gray Leaf Spot on maize in your region. Foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins) are used in severe cases — consult local agricultural extension for registered options, rates, and application timing.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: If disease progresses above the ear leaf before grain fill (R2–R3), yield loss may be severe. Contact extension officer for economic threshold assessment.

source_references.organization: CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center)

corn_leaf_blight.scientific_name: Exserohilum turcicum (Pass.) K.J. Leonard & Suggs (formerly Helminthosporium turcicum)
corn_leaf_blight.leaf_symptoms: Large, cigar-shaped (elliptical) tan-brown lesions 2.5–15 cm long with regular tan or grayish coloring. Lesions have wavy, irregular margins (not vein-constrained). Sporulation produces an olive-green to grayish mass of conidia on lesion surface under humid conditions.
corn_leaf_blight.stem_symptoms: Husk and sheath lesions possible in severe infections.
corn_leaf_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Husk leaves may show lesions in severe cases.
corn_leaf_blight.early_symptoms: Small, elliptical pale green to grayish water-soaked lesions on lower leaves.
corn_leaf_blight.advanced_symptoms: Large cigar-shaped lesions (up to 15 cm). Lesions coalesce causing complete leaf blight. Disease progresses from lower to upper canopy.
corn_leaf_blight.visual_appearance: Long tan-brown cigar-shaped lesions on both leaf surfaces. Lesions do not respect vein boundaries (distinguishing from Gray Leaf Spot).
corn_leaf_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Cigar-shaped (fusiform) large tan lesions on maize leaves — a key diagnostic feature. Olive-gray sporulation visible in humid conditions.
lookalike_conditions: Southern Corn Leaf Blight (smaller, more elongated lesions)
corn_leaf_blight.visual_differentiation: NCLB lesions are large, cigar-shaped, and NOT bounded by veins; GLS lesions are rectangular and constrained by veins.
corn_leaf_blight.disease_cycle_summary: E. turcicum overwinters in crop residue. Conidia released under moisture conditions are dispersed by wind. Infection requires 6–18 hours of continuous leaf wetness. Disease progresses from lower to upper canopy.
corn_leaf_blight.spread_mechanism: Wind dispersal of conidia from infected crop residue.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Cool to moderate temperatures (18–27°C) favor infection. Optimal sporulation at 18–22°C.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity and prolonged leaf wetness are critical. Minimum 6 hours of leaf wetness for infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Rain and dew are critical drivers. Cool nights that maintain dew promote rapid disease development.

corn_leaf_blight.growth_stage_context: Most damaging when infection occurs before tasseling. Ear leaf infection during grain fill is most economically significant.
corn_leaf_blight.monitoring_guidance: Scout at V6–V8 and VT/R1. Assess lesion area on ear leaf and surrounding leaves. Economic threshold typically 5% leaf area infected on ear leaf at tasseling.
corn_leaf_blight.prevention: Plant resistant hybrids (primary strategy). Practice crop rotation with non-host crops. Incorporate residue through tillage where appropriate.
corn_leaf_blight.cultural_management: Crop rotation reduces inoculum. Bury residue. Choose hybrids with NCLB resistance.
corn_leaf_blight.sanitation: Deep plough to incorporate debris. Remove infected plants in small plots.
corn_leaf_blight.water_irrigation_management: Avoid excessive moisture through correct irrigation management.
corn_leaf_blight.crop_rotation: Rotate with soybean, legumes, or cotton to reduce residue-borne inoculum.
corn_leaf_blight.resistant_varieties: NCLB-resistant maize hybrids are available. Consult ICAR-IIMR or seed companies for current resistant hybrid recommendations in your area.
corn_leaf_blight.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE — no established commercial biocontrol in reviewed Indian sources.
corn_leaf_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for NCLB on maize in your region. Consult local extension for registered foliar fungicide options and application timing.
corn_leaf_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: If more than 50% of leaf area above the ear is blighted before grain fill, contact extension officer for yield loss assessment.

corn_rust_leaf.leaf_symptoms: Cinnamon-brown to brick-red oval to elongated pustules (uredia) scattered on both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Pustules are 1–4 mm in diameter and rupture the epidermis, releasing powdery reddish-brown urediniospores. Later in season, pustules may turn dark brown-black (telia).
corn_rust_leaf.stem_symptoms: Leaf sheaths and husks may be affected.
corn_rust_leaf.early_symptoms: Small pale chlorotic flecks visible before pustule eruption. Then small raised powdery cinnamon pustules appear.
corn_rust_leaf.advanced_symptoms: Dense pustules cover large portions of leaf. Leaf tissue around pustules may become chlorotic. Premature senescence.
corn_rust_leaf.visual_appearance: Brick-red raised powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces. When numerous, leaves appear rusty or orange-brown.
corn_rust_leaf.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Powdery reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces — characteristic of rust infections. Pustules erupt through leaf epidermis.
lookalike_conditions: Southern Rust (Puccinia polysora — pustules mainly on upper leaf surface, orange, smaller, more densely packed)
Common bunt (different crop stage and appearance)
corn_rust_leaf.visual_differentiation: Common rust: pustules on both surfaces, brick-red color. Southern rust: pustules predominantly on upper surface, more orange-colored, very dense.
corn_rust_leaf.disease_cycle_summary: Puccinia sorghi requires two hosts: maize (uredial/telial stage) and Oxalis spp. (aecial stage). In tropical regions, urediniospores cycle continuously on maize without the alternate host. Spread by wind over long distances.
corn_rust_leaf.spread_mechanism: Airborne dispersal of urediniospores over long distances.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Optimal temperature for infection is 15–20°C with mild conditions. Temperatures above 30°C slow development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity and free moisture on leaf surface (dew, rain) for 6–12 hours are required for spore germination.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rain events and dew promote infection. Disease more severe in elevated or highland areas with cooler temperatures.

corn_rust_leaf.growth_stage_context: Most damaging if infection occurs at tasseling (VT) or early grain fill (R1). Late season infection is generally less economically important.
corn_rust_leaf.monitoring_guidance: Scout for early pustules on ear leaves and lower leaves at V8–VT. Economic threshold varies by hybrid resistance and stage — consult local extension.
corn_rust_leaf.prevention: Plant resistant hybrids (most effective strategy). Avoid planting susceptible hybrids in areas with historically high rust pressure.
corn_rust_leaf.cultural_management: Early planting to reduce coincidence with disease-favorable conditions. Resistant hybrids are primary management.
corn_rust_leaf.sanitation: NOT_APPLICABLE — rust dispersal is airborne and long-distance; field sanitation has limited impact on common rust.
corn_rust_leaf.water_irrigation_management: Avoid irrigation methods that keep canopy wet for extended periods.
corn_rust_leaf.crop_rotation: NOT_APPLICABLE for common rust — inoculum arrives by wind from external sources.
corn_rust_leaf.resistant_varieties: Resistant hybrids are the primary management strategy. Consult ICAR-IIMR or regional seed companies for current rust-resistant maize hybrids.
corn_rust_leaf.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for maize rust in your region. Foliar fungicide application at early tasseling may be warranted on susceptible hybrids — consult local extension for registered options and economic threshold guidance.
corn_rust_leaf.expert_escalation_conditions: If pustule coverage exceeds 25% of ear leaf area at tasseling, consult extension for fungicide decision guidance.

cotton_bacterial_blight.scientific_name: Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum (Smith) Dye (formerly Xanthomonas campestris pv. malvacearum)
cotton_bacterial_blight.leaf_symptoms: Water-soaked angular lesions constrained by leaf veins. Lesions turn dark brown to black (giving 'blackarm' appearance on stems). Under humid conditions, bacterial ooze may be visible. Older lesions dry out and become papery.
cotton_bacterial_blight.stem_symptoms: Dark angular, water-soaked lesions on stems and petioles progressing to blackening ('blackarm'). Infected stems may crack and ooze bacterial exudate.
cotton_bacterial_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Dark, sunken lesions on bolls. Infected bolls may not open; internal lint is stained. Boll rot can result from secondary infections.
cotton_bacterial_blight.early_symptoms: Small water-soaked translucent spots on seedling cotyledons or true leaves, angular and constrained by veins.
cotton_bacterial_blight.advanced_symptoms: Large necrotic angular dark lesions on leaves. Premature defoliation. Blackened stems. Boll infection.
cotton_bacterial_blight.visual_appearance: Dark brown to black angular leaf lesions with a water-soaked margin. Angular vein-bounded pattern is distinctive.
cotton_bacterial_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Angular (vein-bounded) water-soaked lesions that turn black. Blackening of stems/petioles ('blackarm') is highly distinctive.
cotton_bacterial_blight.visual_differentiation: Angular blackened lesions bounded by leaf veins; 'blackarm' on stems are diagnostic. Fungal spots are circular/irregular, not angular.
cotton_bacterial_blight.disease_cycle_summary: Pathogen survives in infected seed and crop debris. Spread by rain splash, wind, irrigation, and infected seed. Infection occurs through stomata and wounds during wet weather.
cotton_bacterial_blight.spread_mechanism: Rain splash, contaminated seed, irrigation water, farm equipment, and insects.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (25–35°C) combined with wet conditions promote infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity (>80%) and free moisture on leaves are required for infection and spread.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Periods of frequent rain especially at seedling stage are most dangerous. Thunderstorms create wounds that allow entry.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — no specific soil association documented.

cotton_bacterial_blight.growth_stage_context: Seedling stage is most vulnerable. Infection at flowering/boll development causes significant yield loss through boll rot.
cotton_bacterial_blight.monitoring_guidance: Inspect seedlings and leaf canopy weekly after rains. Blackarm symptoms on stems require immediate action. Monitor seed sources for bacterial contamination.
cotton_bacterial_blight.prevention: Use certified disease-free or treated seeds. Practice crop rotation. Avoid working in fields when plants are wet. Remove infected plant debris after harvest.
cotton_bacterial_blight.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected plant material. Avoid overhead irrigation. Space plants correctly for canopy airflow.
cotton_bacterial_blight.sanitation: Deep ploughing of infected debris. Do not save seed from infected crops. Disinfect farm tools.
cotton_bacterial_blight.water_irrigation_management: Use furrow or drip irrigation. Avoid flood irrigation that spreads contaminated water. Avoid overhead irrigation.
cotton_bacterial_blight.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals or other non-host crops for at least 2 seasons.
cotton_bacterial_blight.resistant_varieties: Resistant cotton varieties have been developed. Consult ICAR-CICR (Central Institute for Cotton Research) or state agricultural universities for current resistant variety recommendations.
cotton_bacterial_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for cotton bacterial blight in your region. Copper-based bactericides are commonly referenced — consult local agricultural extension for registered options, rates, and timing.
cotton_bacterial_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: Blackarm on stems combined with boll infection warrants immediate expert consultation. Affected seed lots should not be used for planting.

cotton_healthy.leaf_symptoms: No visible symptoms. Leaves are dark green, firm, and structurally intact.
cotton_healthy.visual_appearance: Uniform deep green leaves with intact lobed structure.
cotton_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy cotton leaves show no angular spots, no curling, and no blackening.
cotton_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly for early symptoms of leaf curl virus (upward curling, vein thickening) and bacterial blight (angular spots). Monitor whitefly and sucking pest populations regularly.
cotton_healthy.prevention: Use certified disease-free planting material. Control whitefly populations to prevent Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuV). Maintain balanced fertilization and proper irrigation.
cotton_healthy.cultural_management: Maintain field hygiene. Remove and destroy host weeds. Ensure proper crop spacing.
cotton_healthy.sanitation: Remove cotton crop debris after harvest. Deep plough to bury residue.
cotton_healthy.water_irrigation_management: Avoid waterlogging. Cotton is sensitive to both drought and excess moisture.
cotton_healthy.crop_rotation: Rotate with wheat, sorghum, or legumes.
cotton_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE for general advice — consult ICAR-CICR for current recommendations.

cotton_leaf_curl_virus.scientific_name: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuV) — a complex of Begomoviruses; most damaging is Cotton Leaf Curl Kokhran Virus (CLCuKoV) associated with CLCuMuB betasatellite
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.pathogen_or_cause: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus complex (CLCuV), transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci (Genn.)
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.leaf_symptoms: Upward curling of leaves (primary diagnostic feature). Thickening, darkening, and enation (outgrowths) on underside of leaf veins. Leaf becomes cup-shaped with curled margins. Vein swelling and leaf thickening are characteristic.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.stem_symptoms: Stem enations and curling. Internodes shorten. Plant is stunted.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Fewer and smaller bolls. Boll quality is poor.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.early_symptoms: Upward curling of young leaves. Mild darkening and thickening of leaf veins.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.advanced_symptoms: Severe upward curling of most leaves. Pronounced vein thickening and enation on lower surface. Severe stunting. Drastically reduced boll production.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.visual_appearance: Upward-curled, cup-shaped leaves with prominent thickened/enated veins on underside. Dark green leaves.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Upward leaf curl PLUS dark enations (raised ridges/warts) on the underside of leaf veins is pathognomonic for CLCuD. Distinguished from nutritional curl by these vein enations.
lookalike_conditions: Physiological leaf curl (from water stress — no enations)
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.visual_differentiation: CLCuD: upward curl WITH distinct vein thickening and enations on underside. Physiological curl from stress: no enations, leaf returns to normal when stress relieved.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.disease_cycle_summary: CLCuV survives in infected plants and weed hosts. Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) transmits the virus persistently (circulative manner). The virus cannot be transmitted by seed, mechanical contact, or other means. Whitefly population explosions in hot dry conditions drive epidemic spread.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.spread_mechanism: Exclusively vector-transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Persistent, circulative transmission — whitefly acquires virus in 24–48 hours of feeding and can transmit for its lifetime.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: High temperatures (30–40°C) favor whitefly population growth and virus spread. CLCuD epidemics are most severe in hot dry conditions.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: Low-moderate humidity favors whitefly multiplication. High humidity reduces whitefly activity.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Dry weather periods favor whitefly build-up and CLCuD spread.

cotton_leaf_curl_virus.growth_stage_context: Plants are susceptible throughout vegetative stages. Infection before 60 days of growth causes severe yield loss. Late infections (after bolls are set) cause less yield loss.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.monitoring_guidance: Monitor whitefly populations using yellow sticky traps (2 per acre). Inspect growing tips and undersides of young leaves. Scout border rows first as whitefly colonizes edges first.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.prevention: Plant resistant varieties (most important strategy). Use CLCuV-resistant cotton varieties recommended for your region. Raise nursery under net protection. Remove and destroy weed hosts (e.g., Malvaceous weeds). Control whitefly with reflective mulches. Avoid off-season cotton cultivation that maintains whitefly populations year-round.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.cultural_management: Rogue out severely infected plants early. Remove alternate host weeds around field. Avoid planting near other CLCuD-infected crops.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.sanitation: Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest. Uproot ratoon cotton.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.water_irrigation_management: Maintain plant vigor with adequate irrigation to avoid stress that may increase susceptibility.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.crop_rotation: Avoid continuous cotton. Rotate with non-host crops.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.resistant_varieties: Several CLCuD-resistant and tolerant cotton varieties have been developed in India. Consult ICAR-CICR, Punjab Agricultural University (PAU), or local KVK for current resistant variety recommendations for your location.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.biological_control: Encourage natural enemies of whitefly. Neem-based products have been used as a component of IPM for whitefly management — consult product label and local extension.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for whitefly control on cotton in your region. Systemic insecticides are used for whitefly management — consult local agricultural extension or product label for registered options and rates. Rotate insecticide classes to prevent resistance.
cotton_leaf_curl_virus.expert_escalation_conditions: If more than 20% plants show severe symptoms within 60 days of sowing, consult agricultural extension immediately. Widespread CLCuD may indicate a new, more virulent virus strain.

groundnut_early_leaf_spot.scientific_name: Cercosporidium personatum (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) Deighton (teleomorph: Mycosphaerella berkeleyi)
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.pathogen_or_cause: Cercospora arachidicola S.Hori (Early Leaf Spot) — Note: Cercosporidium personatum causes Late Leaf Spot; these are often confused but symptom distinction is possible
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.leaf_symptoms: Circular brown spots with a distinctive yellow halo on the UPPER leaf surface. Spots are dark brown to black (darker on upper surface). Gray-white sporulation may appear on the lower leaf surface. Spots typically 1–10 mm diameter.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.stem_symptoms: Spots on stems and petioles causing defoliation in severe cases.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Spot-like lesions on pods in severe cases.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.early_symptoms: Small pale yellowish spots (2–4 mm) on upper leaf surface.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.advanced_symptoms: Spots enlarge and turn dark brown with prominent yellow halos. Mass defoliation from lower canopy upward. Stems appear bare.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.visual_appearance: Dark brown circular spots WITH YELLOW HALOS on the upper leaf surface — the yellow halo is a distinguishing feature from Late Leaf Spot.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Dark brown spots with YELLOW HALOS on upper leaf surface; sporulation predominantly on LOWER surface.
lookalike_conditions: groundnut_late_leaf_spot (similar spots but without prominent yellow halo; sporulation predominantly on lower surface in Late)
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.visual_differentiation: Early Leaf Spot: dark brown spots WITH yellow halo (upper surface). Late Leaf Spot: dark/black spots WITHOUT prominent yellow halo, sporulation on lower surface, appears later in season.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.disease_cycle_summary: Fungus survives in infected crop debris and volunteer plants. Spores spread by wind and rain splash. Multiple infection cycles per season under humid conditions.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash of conidia.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Temperature range 25–30°C is most favorable. Infection impaired at temperatures above 33°C or below 15°C.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity (>80%) and leaf wetness are required. Disease develops faster with dew or rain.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Prolonged wet spells (particularly during rainy season in Kharif crop) promote rapid disease spread.

groundnut_early_leaf_spot.growth_stage_context: Disease appears from 30–35 days after sowing, with maximum severity from 60–80 DAS. Can cause 50–70% yield loss if not managed.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.monitoring_guidance: Begin scouting at 30 DAS. Record incidence (% plants infected) and severity (% leaf area affected). Threshold may be set at 5–10% incidence — consult local extension for spray threshold.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.prevention: Use disease-free certified seed. Plant disease-tolerant varieties. Avoid water stress during critical growth stages. Proper spacing for airflow.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected debris after harvest. Practice crop rotation.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.sanitation: Deep ploughing to bury infected crop debris. Remove volunteer groundnut plants.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.water_irrigation_management: Avoid excessive irrigation that creates prolonged high humidity. Irrigate in the morning.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals or other non-host crops for 1–2 seasons.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.resistant_varieties: Several varieties with partial resistance are available. Consult ICRISAT or state agricultural universities (ANGRAU, TNAU) for current resistant variety recommendations for your region.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE from reviewed Indian sources for practical commercial use.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for groundnut leaf spot in your region. Chlorothalonil, mancozeb-based products, and carbendazim are commonly referenced in Indian extension literature — consult local agricultural extension for current registered options, rates, and spray intervals.
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: If defoliation exceeds 40–50% by 70–80 DAS, contact agricultural extension officer for guidance.

source_references.organization: ICRISAT (International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics)

groundnut_healthy.leaf_symptoms: Leaves are green, pinnately compound, with four leaflets. Margins are entire with no lesions, spots, or pustules.
groundnut_healthy.visual_appearance: Uniform green pinnate leaves with no visible spots, pustules, or yellowing.
groundnut_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy groundnut leaves have no circular spots, no orange pustules, and no yellowing of leaf tissue.
groundnut_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly from 30 DAS. Check for first appearance of leaf spots on lower leaves. Monitor for rust pustules (orange) on underside of leaves.
groundnut_healthy.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed. Choose tolerant varieties. Maintain correct plant spacing. Practice crop rotation.
groundnut_healthy.cultural_management: Maintain field hygiene. Remove weeds. Avoid waterlogging.
groundnut_healthy.sanitation: Remove crop debris after harvest. Deep plough infected debris.
groundnut_healthy.water_irrigation_management: Avoid waterlogging. Maintain adequate moisture during peg development and pod fill.
groundnut_healthy.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals (rice, sorghum, maize) to break disease cycle.
groundnut_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE for general advice — consult ICRISAT or ICAR-NRCG.

groundnut_late_leaf_spot.scientific_name: Cercosporidium personatum (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) Deighton (anamorphic; teleomorph: Mycosphaerella berkeleyi W.A. Jenkins)
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.leaf_symptoms: Dark brown to black circular spots on the LOWER leaf surface. Spots are smaller and darker than Early Leaf Spot and lack the prominent yellow halo. Sporulation (dark tufts) is visible on the lower leaf surface. Upper surface shows dark spots without distinct halo.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.stem_symptoms: Lesions on stems and petioles leading to defoliation.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Pod lesions possible in severe infections.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.early_symptoms: Dark spots appear later in the crop season (60–80+ DAS). Initially similar to early leaf spot but darker.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.advanced_symptoms: Dense black spots without yellow halos. Rapid defoliation. Premature drying.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.visual_appearance: Dark/black circular spots, primarily on LOWER leaf surface, with dark sporulation (tufts or powdery mass). NO prominent yellow halo.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Black spots with sporulation predominantly on LOWER leaf surface; appears later in the season than Early Leaf Spot.
lookalike_conditions: groundnut_early_leaf_spot (similar but with prominent yellow halo)
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.visual_differentiation: Late Leaf Spot: darker (black) spots, lower surface sporulation, no yellow halo, appears later (>60 DAS). Early Leaf Spot: brown spots with yellow halo, appears earlier (30–35 DAS).
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.disease_cycle_summary: Fungus survives in crop debris. Spores spread by wind and rain. Disease typically appears after Early Leaf Spot. Often co-occurs with Early Leaf Spot causing combined damage.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash dispersal of conidia.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Temperatures of 20–30°C support disease development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: Prolonged leaf wetness and high humidity (>80%) facilitate infection. Rain splash critical for spore dispersal.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Wet and humid conditions from 60 DAS onward promote rapid disease progression.

groundnut_late_leaf_spot.growth_stage_context: Typically appears at 60–80 DAS and can cause severe defoliation from 70–90 DAS affecting pod development and kernel fill.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.monitoring_guidance: Begin scouting at 60 DAS. Both Early and Late Leaf Spot may be present simultaneously. Assess severity on middle canopy leaves.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.prevention: Use tolerant varieties. Practice crop rotation. Properly space plants. Monitor from 30 DAS for early intervention.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.cultural_management: Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest. Rotate crops.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.sanitation: Deep ploughing to bury infected debris.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.water_irrigation_management: Same as for Early Leaf Spot — avoid prolonged canopy wetness.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-host cereals or legumes.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.resistant_varieties: Tolerant varieties available. Consult ICRISAT or ICAR-NRCG for recommendations.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE from reviewed sources for commercial use.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.chemical_control: Same principles as Early Leaf Spot. Consult local extension for registered fungicide options.
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: If defoliation exceeds 50% before crop maturity, contact extension officer.

groundnut_rust.leaf_symptoms: Orange to cinnamon-brown uredinia (pustules) predominantly on the LOWER leaf surface. Pustules are small (0.5–2 mm), round to elongated, and rupture the epidermis, releasing powdery orange-brown urediniospores. Upper leaf surface shows chlorotic (yellow) spots corresponding to pustules below.
groundnut_rust.stem_symptoms: Pustules on stems and petioles in severe infections.
groundnut_rust.early_symptoms: Pale yellow-green flecks on upper leaf surface. Orange pustules erupt on lower surface.
groundnut_rust.advanced_symptoms: Dense orange pustules on lower leaf surface. Premature yellowing and defoliation.
groundnut_rust.visual_appearance: Tiny orange-brown raised pustules predominantly on lower leaf surface; upper surface shows yellow spots. Powdery orange mass released when pustule is rubbed.
groundnut_rust.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Orange powdery pustules predominantly on LOWER LEAF SURFACE, with corresponding chlorotic spots on upper surface. Powder-orange spore mass is diagnostic.
lookalike_conditions: groundnut_early_leaf_spot (circular brown spots, not orange pustules)
groundnut_rust.visual_differentiation: Rust has characteristic orange powdery pustules on leaf undersurface. Leaf spots (early/late) produce discrete circular brown-black lesions without orange spore mass.
groundnut_rust.disease_cycle_summary: Puccinia arachidis survives in infected crop debris and alternate/volunteer hosts. Urediniospores are wind-dispersed and can cause multiple infection cycles during a single season. In India, disease is most severe in the humid Kharif season.
groundnut_rust.spread_mechanism: Wind dispersal of urediniospores. Long-distance spread possible.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Optimal temperature for infection is 20–25°C. Temperatures above 30°C reduce infection rates.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and free moisture (rain, dew) required for spore germination. Minimum 6–10 hours of leaf wetness.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Rainy season (Kharif) with high humidity drives epidemic development in India.

groundnut_rust.growth_stage_context: Disease commonly appears from 45–50 DAS in susceptible varieties. Most damaging during pod development (70–100 DAS). Can cause 50–70% yield loss.
groundnut_rust.monitoring_guidance: Scout from 40–45 DAS. Inspect lower surface of middle-canopy leaves. Record pustule count per leaf. Spray threshold varies — consult local extension.
groundnut_rust.prevention: Plant rust-tolerant/resistant varieties (primary strategy). Practice crop rotation. Ensure proper plant spacing.
groundnut_rust.cultural_management: Use resistant varieties. Timely sowing to avoid peak rust season.
groundnut_rust.sanitation: Remove and destroy infected crop residue. Deep ploughing after harvest.
groundnut_rust.water_irrigation_management: Avoid prolonged wet conditions by using appropriate irrigation methods.
groundnut_rust.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals to reduce inoculum build-up.
groundnut_rust.resistant_varieties: Several rust-tolerant/resistant varieties have been developed at ICRISAT and Indian universities. Consult ICRISAT, ICAR-NRCG, or local KVK for current recommendations.
groundnut_rust.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for groundnut rust in your region. Systemic fungicides are used for rust management — consult local agricultural extension for registered options and timing.
groundnut_rust.expert_escalation_conditions: Severe rust incidence (>50% leaf area affected) before pod maturity warrants expert consultation.

pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria (Doidge) Dye (and related Xanthomonas species including X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri)
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.pathogen_or_cause: Xanthomonas euvesicatoria / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria complex
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.leaf_symptoms: Small (2–5 mm), water-soaked, angular to circular spots on leaf that turn brown to dark brown with yellow halos. Spots may coalesce. In severe cases, large sections of leaf become necrotic and leaves fall prematurely.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.stem_symptoms: Dark elongated lesions on stems and petioles.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Raised, corky or wart-like spots on fruit surface that are initially water-soaked. Fruit lesions provide entry for secondary organisms causing fruit rot.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.early_symptoms: Small water-soaked spots with angular outline on leaves.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.advanced_symptoms: Large, necrotic angular spots with yellow halos. Premature leaf drop. Fruit spot and rot.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.visual_appearance: Angular to circular brown spots with yellow halos on leaves. Wart-like raised spots on fruits.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Angular or circular brown lesions with YELLOW HALOS on leaves; corky raised lesions on fruits are characteristic of bacterial spot.
lookalike_conditions: Anthracnose on pepper (circular sunken spots on fruit, usually without yellow halo on leaves)
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.visual_differentiation: Bacterial spot: angular-to-circular lesions with yellow halos on leaves AND distinctive fruit lesions. Fungal spots generally lack the angular pattern and yellow halo.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.disease_cycle_summary: Bacteria survive in infected seed, plant debris, and soil. Infection occurs through wounds and natural openings. Rain splash and wind are primary spread mechanisms.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.spread_mechanism: Rain splash, contaminated seed, infected transplants, farm equipment, and workers moving through wet fields.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (24–30°C) favor bacterial growth and disease development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and rain splash are essential for spread. Free moisture required for infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rain events facilitate bacteria-laden rain splash. Overhead irrigation exacerbates the disease.

pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.growth_stage_context: All stages susceptible. Early transplant infection causes severe defoliation. Fruit stage infection causes significant market quality loss.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.monitoring_guidance: Inspect transplants before field planting. Scout weekly for leaf spots. Increased scouting after rain events.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free (pathogen-tested) seed. Treat seeds with hot water (50°C for 25 minutes) or bleach solution before planting. Grow disease-free transplants. Avoid overhead irrigation. Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected plant material. Avoid working in wet fields. Disinfect tools between plants.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.sanitation: Destroy infected crop debris. Do not save seed from infected plants.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.water_irrigation_management: Use drip irrigation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Irrigate in morning so leaves dry quickly.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, legumes) for at least 2–3 years.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.resistant_varieties: Some resistant varieties exist. Consult ICAR vegetable research stations or seed companies for current recommendations for your region.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE from reviewed sources for commercial pepper use in India.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for pepper bacterial spot in your region. Copper-based bactericides are commonly referenced — consult local extension for registered options.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: If defoliation is extensive or fruit spots are severe, consult agricultural extension. Copper-resistant strains have been documented in some regions.

pepper_bell_healthy.leaf_symptoms: Leaves are bright green, smooth, with intact margins. No visible spots, lesions, or discoloration.
pepper_bell_healthy.visual_appearance: Smooth bright green leaves with no visible damage.
pepper_bell_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy leaves show no angular lesions, no yellow halos, and no curling.
pepper_bell_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly for bacterial spot symptoms, particularly after rains. Monitor for whiteflies and aphids (virus vectors).
pepper_bell_healthy.prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants. Avoid overhead irrigation. Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants.
pepper_bell_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE for general advice — consult ICAR.

potato_early_blight.scientific_name: Alternaria solani (Ellis & G. Martin) L.R. Jones & Grout
potato_early_blight.leaf_symptoms: Circular to oval, dark brown lesions with distinctive concentric rings creating a 'target-board' or 'bull's-eye' pattern. Lesions often have a YELLOW HALO. Older (lower) leaves are affected first. Lesions can enlarge to 1–2 cm. Severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop.
potato_early_blight.stem_symptoms: Dark brown elongated lesions on stems near soil.
potato_early_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Shallow circular dark brown sunken lesions on tubers, particularly at stem end. Tuber lesions may have a corky dry rot.
potato_early_blight.early_symptoms: Small dark circular spots (2–4 mm) on lower/older leaves with faint concentric rings.
potato_early_blight.advanced_symptoms: Large target-pattern lesions (1–2+ cm), yellow halo, premature defoliation from lower canopy upward.
potato_early_blight.visual_appearance: Brown circular lesions with prominent concentric ring pattern (target board) and yellow halo on older leaves.
potato_early_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: CONCENTRIC RING PATTERN within brown necrotic lesion on older leaves — pathognomonic for Early Blight.
lookalike_conditions: potato_late_blight (water-soaked, rapidly expanding lesions, no concentric rings, affects younger leaves)
Cercospora leaf spot (similar but different crop)
Potassium deficiency (leaf edge burn, no lesions)
potato_early_blight.visual_differentiation: Early Blight: concentric rings, older leaves affected first, brown lesions with yellow halo. Late Blight: irregular water-soaked dark lesions, white sporulation on underside in humid conditions, rapid expansion, no concentric rings.
potato_early_blight.disease_cycle_summary: A. solani overwinters in infected crop debris and contaminated seed tubers. Conidia dispersed by wind and rain splash. Multiple infection cycles per season.
potato_early_blight.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash of conidia from crop debris.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (24–29°C) favor disease development. Unlike Late Blight, Early Blight develops in warmer conditions.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity (>90%) and leaf wetness periods (>3–6 hours) facilitate infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Alternating wet and dry periods can accelerate disease as rain splashes spores and dry conditions stress plants (stressed plants are more susceptible).
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: Soil nutrient deficiency (particularly nitrogen) increases plant susceptibility.

potato_early_blight.growth_stage_context: Disease appears from mid-season (at flowering) when lower leaves begin to senesce. Plants stressed by nutrient deficiency, drought, or other factors are more susceptible.
potato_early_blight.monitoring_guidance: Scout from flowering onwards. Record % plants showing symptoms and % leaf area affected on lower canopy.
potato_early_blight.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers. Select healthy, disease-free planting material. Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops. Plant tolerant varieties. Maintain adequate plant nutrition.
potato_early_blight.cultural_management: Remove infected lower leaves where practical. Avoid plant stress. Use balanced fertilization.
potato_early_blight.sanitation: Remove and destroy infected crop debris after harvest. Avoid dumping infected material in or near fields.
potato_early_blight.water_irrigation_management: Avoid overhead irrigation. Use drip or furrow irrigation. Irrigate in morning.
potato_early_blight.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, pulses) for 2–3 years.
potato_early_blight.resistant_varieties: Tolerant varieties available. Consult ICAR-CPRI (Central Potato Research Institute) for current recommendations for your agro-climatic zone.
potato_early_blight.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE from reviewed sources for commercial use in India.
potato_early_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for potato early blight in your region. Consult ICAR-CPRI or local extension for registered fungicide options and recommended spray schedule.
potato_early_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: If early blight appears before flowering or spreads rapidly despite management, consult agricultural extension.

potato_healthy.leaf_symptoms: Compound leaves with 3–5 leaflets. Dark green color, no lesions, no water-soaked areas.
potato_healthy.visual_appearance: Dark green compound leaves, structurally intact.
potato_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy potato lacks any circular lesions, water-soaked areas, or white sporulation on underside.
potato_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly from tuber initiation. Late Blight monitoring is critical — check leaf undersides for white sporulation after cool humid periods.
potato_healthy.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers. Apply seed treatment. Ensure proper spacing and hilling.
potato_healthy.cultural_management: Maintain balanced nutrition. Avoid water stress.
potato_healthy.sanitation: Destroy volunteer potato plants and infected debris from previous season.
potato_healthy.water_irrigation_management: Use drip or furrow irrigation. Avoid overhead spray.
potato_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE for general advice — consult ICAR-CPRI.

potato_late_blight.pathogen_or_cause: Phytophthora infestans (oomycete — not a true fungus, but managed similarly)
potato_late_blight.leaf_symptoms: Irregular water-soaked, dark-green to brown-black lesions that enlarge rapidly, often with a water-soaked margin at the edge. Characteristic WHITE COTTONY SPORULATION (sporangiophores) visible on the underside of lesions in humid conditions. Lesions appear greasy and water-soaked initially.
potato_late_blight.stem_symptoms: Dark brown, water-soaked lesions on stems that can girdle and kill the plant.
potato_late_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Tubers show reddish-brown irregular dry rot extending from the surface inward. Tuber blight can cause complete tuber loss.
potato_late_blight.early_symptoms: Small pale green to dark water-soaked spots at leaf margin or tip, often with water-soaked border, rapidly expanding.
potato_late_blight.advanced_symptoms: Large dark brown-black necrotic areas covering most of the leaf. White sporulation on leaf underside in humid conditions. Rapid plant collapse.
potato_late_blight.visual_appearance: Irregular, rapidly expanding dark brown to black lesions, often starting at leaf margins or tips. White sporulation on underside in humid conditions.
potato_late_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Rapidly expanding dark water-soaked lesions with WHITE COTTONY SPORULATION on LEAF UNDERSIDE (under humid conditions) — a key diagnostic feature.
lookalike_conditions: potato_early_blight (concentric rings, older leaves, slower progression)
Frost damage (affects entire plant, no sporulation)
potato_late_blight.visual_differentiation: Late Blight: rapidly expanding water-soaked dark lesions, white sporulation on underside in humidity, affects young leaves and stems. Early Blight: concentric rings on older leaves, no rapid expansion, no white underside sporulation.
potato_late_blight.disease_cycle_summary: P. infestans survives in infected tubers (cull piles, volunteer plants). Under cool humid conditions, sporangia are produced and dispersed by wind and rain to form infections rapidly. Disease can destroy a field in 7–10 days under epidemic conditions.
potato_late_blight.spread_mechanism: Airborne sporangia from infected plants and tuber cull piles; rain splash and wind.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Cool temperatures (10–20°C) are optimal for infection. Disease most severe in cool humid highland areas. Temperatures above 30°C arrest sporulation.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity (>90%) for at least 12 hours triggers sporulation and infection. Continuous humid periods are critical.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Prolonged rain periods and high leaf wetness are required. Wallin and Dutch rules (% hours of leaf wetness > threshold) are used as forecasting tools.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: Infected soil can harbor P. infestans from previous season's infected tubers.

potato_late_blight.growth_stage_context: Most devastating during tuber bulking and maturation. Early infection (tuber initiation) can destroy entire crop. Late infection can reduce tuber quality.
potato_late_blight.monitoring_guidance: Use Wallin Disease Severity Value (DSV) or similar forecasting model if available. Scout DAILY during cool humid weather. Check leaf undersides. Risk periods: after rain, with temperatures below 20°C, and RH >90%.
potato_late_blight.prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers. Use resistant varieties. Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants. Separate clean seed from stored infected tubers. Haulm (vine) destruction before harvest reduces tuber infection.
potato_late_blight.cultural_management: Destroy infected plant material immediately. Remove and destroy infected volunteer potato plants. Ensure proper earthing up.
potato_late_blight.sanitation: Destroy infected tubers and crop residue. Remove volunteer potato plants within and around fields.
potato_late_blight.water_irrigation_management: Avoid overhead irrigation. Use drip or furrow. Do not irrigate during cool humid evenings that prolong leaf wetness.
potato_late_blight.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops. Avoid growing tomato in the same field immediately after potato.
potato_late_blight.resistant_varieties: Resistant varieties are available and are the most effective long-term strategy. Consult ICAR-CPRI for current resistant variety recommendations for your region and growing season.
potato_late_blight.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE — biological control for Late Blight is not practically established in Indian extension literature.
potato_late_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for potato late blight in your region. Protectant and systemic fungicides are used — consult ICAR-CPRI or local extension for registered options, timing, and anti-resistance rotation strategies. Preventive application before symptoms appear is key.
potato_late_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: Immediate expert consultation required if Late Blight is confirmed. Disease can destroy entire fields within 7–10 days without intervention. Contact extension officer for emergency spray guidance.

source_references.organization: FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations)

rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.scientific_name: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Ishiyama) Swings et al.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.leaf_symptoms: Water-soaked, translucent lesions starting from leaf margins or tips. Lesions enlarge along the leaf margin with a wavy irregular yellow border. Leaves turn yellow-straw colored from tip downward. On drying, bacterial exudate may form 'dew drops' on lesion margins in humid conditions.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.stem_symptoms: In severe Kresek phase (seedling systemic infection): entire plant wilts and dies. The pathogen enters through root wounds during transplanting.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Panicle infection can cause empty grains.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.early_symptoms: Water-soaked translucent streaks along leaf margin or tip.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.advanced_symptoms: Yellow-straw colored lesions spreading from tip and margins. Entire leaf turns yellow. Grain filling affected.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.visual_appearance: Yellow to straw-colored leaf margins spreading from tip. Wavy irregular lesion border. 'Dew drop' bacterial ooze on leaf surface (visible early morning in humid conditions).
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Straw-yellow lesions extending from the LEAF TIP and MARGINS downward with wavy edges, and bacterial ooze/droplets in humid conditions.
lookalike_conditions: Rice brown spot (circular lesions on leaf)
Nitrogen deficiency (yellowing from tip — no water-soaked margin, no bacterial ooze)
Sheath blight (different pattern — from lower node upward)
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.visual_differentiation: BLB: lesions starting at tip/margin with wavy edge, bacterial ooze, straw-yellow color. Nitrogen deficiency: uniform yellowing from tip, no water-soaked margins. Brown spot: circular discrete lesions scattered on leaf.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.disease_cycle_summary: Xoo survives in soil, infected stubble, and seeds (less important). Bacteria enter through hydathodes (natural openings at leaf margins) or wounds. Heavy rains and flooding spread bacteria rapidly. Insect feeding wounds also provide entry.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.spread_mechanism: Rain splash, flood/irrigation water, wind, infected seed, and insects.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (25–34°C) with optimal at 26–30°C. High temperature combined with high humidity is most favorable.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity (>80%) and free moisture on leaves are required. Morning dew and rain are critical.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Flooding, heavy rain, and cyclonic conditions dramatically increase disease spread and severity. Flood water carries bacteria across fields.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: High soil nitrogen (excessive urea application) increases plant susceptibility by promoting dense succulent growth.

rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.growth_stage_context: Most damaging from tillering to heading stages. Kresek phase affects seedlings. Late infection at heading reduces grain fill.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.monitoring_guidance: Scout from 30 DAS (transplanted) or 45 DAS (direct seeded). Look for tip blight and margin blight. Record percent affected tillers. Check flooded fields immediately after flood events.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.prevention: Use resistant rice varieties (most effective strategy). Use certified disease-free seeds. Treat seeds with plant growth regulators or recommended bactericides where registered. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization (particularly urea). Drain fields after rain events.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.cultural_management: Remove infected plants in Kresek phase. Avoid transplanting into floodwater. Avoid mechanical damage during transplanting.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.sanitation: Remove and burn infected stubble. Drain fields to prevent water-borne spread.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.water_irrigation_management: Avoid continuous flooding when disease risk is high. Drain fields after rain to remove bacteria-laden water. Avoid sharing irrigation water between infected and healthy fields.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.crop_rotation: NOT_APPLICABLE in most rice systems — manage through variety resistance and water management.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.resistant_varieties: Multiple BLB-resistant varieties are available in India. Consult ICAR-IIRR or IRRI for varieties with resistance genes (Xa genes, e.g., Xa21, Xa13) suited to your region. State agricultural universities maintain variety recommendations.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE for commercial use in reviewed Indian extension literature.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for Rice BLB in your region. Some copper-based and other bactericides are used in severe cases — consult local extension for registered options. Note: chemical control has limited efficacy once disease is established.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: Kresek phase (systemic wilt of seedlings) requires immediate expert consultation. Widespread BLB in transplanted fields after flooding warrants urgent field assessment.

rice_brown_spot.scientific_name: Cochliobolus miyabeanus (S. Ito & Kurib.) Drechsler ex Dastur (anamorph: Bipolaris oryzae)
rice_brown_spot.pathogen_or_cause: Bipolaris oryzae (Breda de Haan) Shoemaker (teleomorph: Cochliobolus miyabeanus)
rice_brown_spot.leaf_symptoms: Oval to circular brown spots (1–5 mm) with gray-white centers and brown borders. Spots have a pale yellow halo in susceptible varieties. Spots scattered over the leaf lamina, not concentrated at margins or tip. In severe cases, spots coalesce and cause large necrotic areas.
rice_brown_spot.stem_symptoms: Lesions on glumes (grain covering) cause 'glume discoloration' and grain sterility.
rice_brown_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Glume lesions (chalkiness, discoloration). Infected grain may be sterile or discolored.
rice_brown_spot.early_symptoms: Small oval to circular brown dots (1–2 mm) scattered on leaf surface.
rice_brown_spot.advanced_symptoms: Numerous spots (>100/leaf) coalescing to large necrotic patches. Premature leaf drying.
rice_brown_spot.visual_appearance: Oval/circular brown spots with gray-white centers and distinct brown borders; yellow halo in susceptible varieties. Scattered distribution across leaf lamina.
rice_brown_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Scattered oval/circular brown spots with gray-white centers and brown borders — NOT at margins/tips. Contrast with BLB (margin-based) and blast (diamond-shaped).
lookalike_conditions: Rice leaf blast (diamond/spindle-shaped lesions, gray centers, elongated)
Narrow brown leaf spot (narrower lesions confined to narrow streaks)
rice_brown_spot.visual_differentiation: Brown spot: oval/circular spots scattered on leaf. Blast: diamond-shaped (spindle-shaped) gray lesions with dark borders, not circular. BLB: margin/tip lesions with straw-yellow color.
rice_brown_spot.disease_cycle_summary: Fungus survives in infected seed and crop residue. Spores are wind-dispersed. Disease commonly associated with nutritionally stressed (particularly silica, potassium, manganese) or waterlogged plants.
rice_brown_spot.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash of conidia from infected crop residue and seed.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (25–30°C) with high humidity. Disease severe in areas with nutritional stress.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and leaf wetness (>8 hours) required for spore germination and infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rains favor spore dispersal. Waterlogged conditions increase plant nutritional stress and susceptibility.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: Low soil fertility — particularly silicon, potassium, and manganese deficiency — dramatically increases susceptibility. Well-known to be a disease associated with nutrient-stressed plants.

rice_brown_spot.growth_stage_context: Can occur from seedling to maturity. Most damaging during booting and heading when grain is filling. Severe at later stages in nutrient-poor soils.
rice_brown_spot.monitoring_guidance: Scout for spots from 30 DAS. Count spots per leaf on 10 plants. Apply disease severity scale (% leaf area affected). Check soil fertility records.
rice_brown_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed. Treat seeds with recommended fungicide/hot water (52°C for 10 minutes). Optimize soil nutrition — apply recommended silicon, potassium, and nitrogen rates. Avoid water stress and waterlogging. Plant tolerant varieties.
rice_brown_spot.cultural_management: Correct soil nutrient deficiencies. Avoid high nitrogen with low potassium/silicon.
rice_brown_spot.sanitation: Remove infected crop residue. Use healthy seed.
rice_brown_spot.water_irrigation_management: Avoid waterlogging and prolonged flooding. Maintain proper drainage.
rice_brown_spot.crop_rotation: NOT_APPLICABLE for most lowland rice systems. Management is primarily through nutrition and variety.
rice_brown_spot.resistant_varieties: Varieties with partial resistance available. Consult ICAR-IIRR or IRRI for current recommendations.
rice_brown_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE for commercial use in reviewed sources.
rice_brown_spot.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for rice brown spot in your region. Seed treatment and foliar fungicides at boot stage may be warranted — consult local extension.
rice_brown_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: Brown spot along with poor grain fill (empty panicles) warrants soil testing and expert consultation on nutrient management.

rice_healthy.leaf_symptoms: Leaves are flat, dark green, linear with a distinct midrib. No lesions, spots, or water-soaked areas visible.
rice_healthy.visual_appearance: Flat dark green linear leaves with intact margins and no visible spots.
rice_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy rice leaves show no circular spots, no water-soaked margin lesions, and no diamond-shaped blast lesions.
rice_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly. Priority diseases to watch: leaf blast, bacterial leaf blight, sheath blight. Inspect leaf sheaths for sheath blight symptoms.
rice_healthy.prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds. Treat seeds before planting. Apply balanced nutrition. Use recommended plant spacing.
rice_healthy.cultural_management: Field hygiene. Remove weeds. Proper water management.
rice_healthy.sanitation: Burn or deep-plough infected crop residue.
rice_healthy.water_irrigation_management: Maintain alternate wet and dry irrigation where appropriate. Avoid prolonged flooding under blast pressure.
rice_healthy.crop_rotation: Where possible, rotate with legumes or other non-rice crops.
rice_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE for general advice — consult ICAR-IIRR or IRRI.

rice_leaf_blast.scientific_name: Magnaporthe oryzae B.C. Couch (anamorph: Pyricularia oryzae Cavara)
rice_leaf_blast.leaf_symptoms: Diamond-shaped (spindle-shaped) to irregular lesions with gray-white centers and dark brown to reddish-brown borders. Lesions may have yellow halos in susceptible varieties. Leaf blast lesions are typically 1–3 cm long and 0.3–0.5 cm wide. In acute phase: small water-soaked spots that expand rapidly into spindle-shaped lesions.
rice_leaf_blast.stem_symptoms: Node blast: dark brown to black discoloration of nodes. Neck blast: infection at panicle neck causing 'rotten neck' — panicle breaks at infected node and hangs down (gray-white).
rice_leaf_blast.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Panicle and grain infection causing empty or poorly filled grains.
rice_leaf_blast.early_symptoms: Small, water-soaked, whitish spots (1–2 mm) on leaves under acute infection conditions.
rice_leaf_blast.advanced_symptoms: Numerous diamond-shaped gray lesions with dark borders coalescing to kill leaf. Neck blast causes white panicles (resembling deadheart from stem borers).
rice_leaf_blast.visual_appearance: DIAMOND-SHAPED (spindle-shaped) gray lesions with brown borders; may have yellow halo. Lesions aligned along leaf axis.
rice_leaf_blast.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Diamond/spindle-shaped gray lesions with DARK REDDISH-BROWN MARGINS — highly distinctive for rice blast. 'Rotten neck' (hanging empty panicle) at reproductive stage.
lookalike_conditions: Brown leaf spot (oval, no distinct diamond-shape)
rice_leaf_blast.visual_differentiation: Blast: diamond-shaped gray lesions with dark borders, aligned along leaf. Brown spot: oval/circular spots, scattered, not diamond-shaped.
rice_leaf_blast.disease_cycle_summary: M. oryzae survives in infected crop residue, seeds, and weedy hosts. Spores (conidia) are dispersed at night under high humidity. Infection requires 8–24 hours of continuous leaf wetness. Disease can cycle many times in a season.
rice_leaf_blast.spread_mechanism: Wind-dispersed conidia released at night under high humidity and dew conditions.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Cool to moderate temperatures (20–28°C) favor infection. Optimal: 24–28°C. Temperatures above 32°C reduce sporulation.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity (>90%) for 6–12 hours and dew formation are critical for spore germination. Dew periods at night are especially important.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Cool, rainy weather with extended night dew is the classic blast epidemic condition. High altitude, upland, and rainfed environments are most at risk.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: Excessive or imbalanced nitrogen (especially urea) promotes succulent growth highly susceptible to blast. Silicon deficiency significantly increases susceptibility.

rice_leaf_blast.growth_stage_context: Leaf blast: most damaging from tillering to panicle initiation. Neck blast: most devastating at heading/flowering (Z65–Z75). A single neck blast infection on a tiller causes complete yield loss of that tiller.
rice_leaf_blast.monitoring_guidance: Scout from tillering. Use blast forecasting models based on temperature and humidity if available. Inspect leaf blade for diamond-shaped lesions. At heading, inspect panicle necks for dark lesions.
rice_leaf_blast.prevention: Plant resistant/tolerant varieties (primary management). Use certified disease-free seeds. Treat seeds with recommended seed treatment. Avoid excessive nitrogen; split nitrogen application; increase potassium. Apply silicon through silicate fertilizers where soil silicon is deficient. Avoid over-irrigating during dew-favorable nights.
rice_leaf_blast.cultural_management: Reduce nitrogen at risk periods (panicle initiation). Alter planting date to avoid peak blast risk period in your area. Drain fields temporarily to reduce humidity.
rice_leaf_blast.sanitation: Destroy infected crop residue. Use certified blast-free seed.
rice_leaf_blast.water_irrigation_management: Maintain thin flood during risk periods to moderate temperature. Alternating wet-dry irrigation can reduce blast pressure in some conditions.
