rice_leaf_blast.crop_rotation: NOT_APPLICABLE for lowland rice. Upland rice rotation with non-grass crops may help reduce inoculum.
rice_leaf_blast.resistant_varieties: Blast-resistant varieties are a key management strategy. Rice blast is highly racially diverse — varieties resistant in one area may not be resistant in another. Consult ICAR-IIRR, IRRI, or state agricultural universities for current variety recommendations for your specific region.
rice_leaf_blast.biological_control: Some Trichoderma and Pseudomonas-based biocontrol products are in experimental and commercial use in India — consult ICAR-IIRR and local extension for registered products.
rice_leaf_blast.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for rice blast in your region. Systemic fungicides (e.g., tricyclazole class) are registered for blast in India — consult ICAR-IIRR or local extension for current registered options, rates, and timing. Preventive application is critical at panicle initiation.
rice_leaf_blast.expert_escalation_conditions: Neck blast confirmed or suspected at heading warrants IMMEDIATE expert consultation. Preventive fungicide at PI stage is critical in blast-endemic areas.

rice_leaf_scald.scientific_name: Microdochium oryzae (Hashioka & Yokogi) Samuels & I.C. Hallett (formerly Helminthosporium oryzae var. minor; Gerlachia oryzae)
rice_leaf_scald.leaf_symptoms: Characteristic zonate (banded) lesions with alternating light tan/straw and dark brown-reddish bands, running ACROSS the leaf width rather than as discrete spots. Lesions typically start from the leaf tip and progress downward. The banded pattern gives a 'scalded' appearance.
rice_leaf_scald.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Grain discoloration possible in severe cases.
rice_leaf_scald.early_symptoms: Light tan banded lesions starting at the leaf tip.
rice_leaf_scald.advanced_symptoms: Large zonate lesions with alternating tan and dark bands killing the leaf blade from tip downward.
rice_leaf_scald.visual_appearance: Zonate (alternating light and dark bands) lesions running transversely across the leaf blade from tip.
rice_leaf_scald.distinctive_symptom_pattern: BANDED/ZONATE pattern on leaf — alternating light tan and dark brown bands running across the leaf width. This distinguishes leaf scald from brown spot (circular spots) and blast (diamond shapes).
lookalike_conditions: Physiological leaf scorch (tip burn from K deficiency or salinity — no banding)
rice_leaf_scald.visual_differentiation: Leaf scald: banded/zonate pattern transverse to leaf. Brown spot: circular scattered spots. Blast: diamond-shaped lesions.
rice_leaf_scald.disease_cycle_summary: M. oryzae survives in infected crop residue and soil. Disease is commonly found in areas with high nitrogen, high humidity, and warm conditions. Often a secondary/opportunistic pathogen.
rice_leaf_scald.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash of conidia from infected debris.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (25–30°C) in combination with high humidity.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Rainy conditions and high humidity promote disease.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — however, excessive nitrogen application has been associated with increased susceptibility in literature.

rice_leaf_scald.growth_stage_context: Disease more common from tillering to maturity stages.
rice_leaf_scald.monitoring_guidance: Scout from tillering. Look for banded zonate lesions starting at leaf tips.
rice_leaf_scald.prevention: Use balanced fertilization (avoid excessive nitrogen). Plant tolerant varieties. Practice good water management.
rice_leaf_scald.cultural_management: Balanced nitrogen management. Remove infected crop residue.
rice_leaf_scald.sanitation: Remove infected crop debris after harvest.
rice_leaf_scald.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE — consult ICAR-IIRR or local extension.
rice_leaf_scald.chemical_control: Use only products registered/labeled for rice leaf scald in your region. Consult local extension.
rice_leaf_scald.expert_escalation_conditions: If symptoms spread rapidly, contact extension officer.
rice_leaf_scald.knowledge_notes: Rice leaf scald is less extensively documented in Indian extension literature compared to blast or BLB. Evidence cited from IRRI and peer-reviewed literature.

rice_sheath_blight.scientific_name: Rhizoctonia solani Kühn AG-1 IA (teleomorph: Thanatephorus cucumeris)
rice_sheath_blight.pathogen_or_cause: Rhizoctonia solani Kühn (Anastomosis Group AG-1 IA)
rice_sheath_blight.leaf_symptoms: Upper leaf blade lesions appear as irregular water-soaked greenish-gray to straw-colored patches with dark brown to purple borders. Lesions on leaves arise from infection spreading up from infected sheath.
rice_sheath_blight.stem_symptoms: Leaf sheath lesions are the primary diagnostic feature: elliptical or irregular lesions on lower leaf sheaths near water line, with grayish-green centers, dark brown borders, and sometimes a white mycelium visible. Sclerotia (small brown fungal bodies) visible at lesion surface.
rice_sheath_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Panicle sheaths may be affected in severe infections.
rice_sheath_blight.early_symptoms: Elliptical, water-soaked greenish-gray spots on leaf sheath at or just above the water line.
rice_sheath_blight.advanced_symptoms: Lesions enlarge and coalesce, covering large portions of sheath and moving upward to upper sheaths and blades. Sclerotia (round, brown, 2–5 mm fungal bodies) visible on infected sheaths.
rice_sheath_blight.visual_appearance: Elliptical gray-straw patches with dark brown borders on leaf sheaths, starting at water line and progressing upward. Brown sclerotia at lesion surface.
rice_sheath_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Elliptical sheath lesions starting AT OR ABOVE WATERLINE progressing upward, with brown SCLEROTIA (small tan-brown round bodies) at lesion surface — diagnostic.
lookalike_conditions: rice_bacterial_leaf_blight (affects margins/tips of leaf lamina, not sheath near waterline)
Sheath rot (different organism, lesions further up sheath, often with grain discoloration)
rice_sheath_blight.visual_differentiation: Sheath Blight: elliptical sheath lesions at waterline progressing upward, sclerotia present. BLB: tip/margin lesions on leaf lamina, straw color, bacterial ooze.
rice_sheath_blight.disease_cycle_summary: R. solani survives as sclerotia in soil and infected crop debris. Sclerotia float on water and infect sheaths at the waterline. Under humid conditions, mycelium spreads rapidly from plant to plant.
rice_sheath_blight.spread_mechanism: Floating sclerotia in water, wind-blown mycelium fragments. Spreads plant-to-plant through direct contact of infected and healthy tillers.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (28–32°C) are optimal. Disease severe in hot humid growing environments.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity (>90%) strongly favors rapid disease development. Humidity near the water surface is particularly important.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Warm humid conditions, standing water, and dense planting drive epidemic development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: High soil nitrogen (especially excessive urea) dramatically increases sheath blight severity by promoting dense, humid canopies.

rice_sheath_blight.growth_stage_context: Most damaging from active tillering to grain fill. Dense plant populations at high nitrogen inputs dramatically increase severity.
rice_sheath_blight.monitoring_guidance: Scout from active tillering onwards. Examine lower leaf sheaths at water level. Record % plants infected and lesion height relative to flag leaf. Sheath blight severity index is used in research.
rice_sheath_blight.prevention: Reduce plant density (wider row/plant spacing — critical in direct seeded rice). Avoid excessive nitrogen (split applications, avoid late urea). Choose partially resistant varieties. Seed treatment where appropriate.
rice_sheath_blight.cultural_management: Reduce plant density. Balanced nitrogen management. Avoid high-density seeding. Collect and remove floating sclerotia from irrigation inlet water.
rice_sheath_blight.sanitation: Remove crop residue and burn. Deep plough to bury sclerotia. Drain and dry field between crop seasons.
rice_sheath_blight.water_irrigation_management: Drain field periodically (intermittent flooding) to reduce humidity near crop base and expose sclerotia to desiccation.
rice_sheath_blight.crop_rotation: Rotation helps reduce sclerotia in soil over time. Consult local extension for appropriate rotation crops.
rice_sheath_blight.resistant_varieties: No completely resistant variety is available, but varieties with partial resistance exist. Consult ICAR-IIRR or state agricultural universities for current recommendations.
rice_sheath_blight.biological_control: Trichoderma harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescens products are used in India as biocontrol agents for sheath blight in integration with fungicide management — consult ICAR-IIRR for registered products and protocols.
rice_sheath_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for rice sheath blight in your region. Consult ICAR-IIRR or local extension for registered fungicide options, rates, and application timing at panicle initiation.
rice_sheath_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: If sheath blight lesions reach flag leaf before heading, yield loss may be >20%. Consult extension officer for management adjustment.

tomato_bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas vesicatoria and related Xanthomonas species (X. euvesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri)
tomato_bacterial_spot.pathogen_or_cause: Xanthomonas vesicatoria and related Xanthomonas spp.
tomato_bacterial_spot.leaf_symptoms: Small (1–3 mm), water-soaked angular to circular spots that turn dark brown with a yellow halo. Lesions may have a water-soaked margin. Spots may have scab-like raised centers. Severe infection leads to defoliation.
tomato_bacterial_spot.stem_symptoms: Dark elongated stem lesions. Petiole lesions cause premature defoliation.
tomato_bacterial_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Raised, water-soaked spots on fruits turning dark and scab-like with corky centers. Fruit lesions cause unmarketable quality.
tomato_bacterial_spot.early_symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit.
tomato_bacterial_spot.advanced_symptoms: Numerous necrotic spots, severe defoliation, scab-like fruit lesions.
tomato_bacterial_spot.visual_appearance: Angular-to-circular brown spots with yellow halos on leaves; scab-like spots on fruits.
tomato_bacterial_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Water-soaked, angular leaf spots with yellow halos; corky/scabby fruit lesions.
tomato_bacterial_spot.visual_differentiation: Bacterial spot: water-soaked angular spots with yellow halo, fruit lesions. Early blight: concentric rings on older leaves. Septoria: circular spots with tiny dark pycnidia in center.
tomato_bacterial_spot.disease_cycle_summary: Bacteria survive on infected seed, plant debris. Spread by rain splash, wind, workers, and tools. Infection through stomata and wounds during wet, warm conditions.
tomato_bacterial_spot.spread_mechanism: Rain splash, contaminated seed, infected transplants, tools, workers in wet fields.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (25–30°C) are most favorable.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and free moisture on leaf surface required.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rain and overhead irrigation promote rapid spread.

tomato_bacterial_spot.growth_stage_context: All stages susceptible. Most economically damaging at fruiting stage.
tomato_bacterial_spot.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly. Increase monitoring after rain events.
tomato_bacterial_spot.prevention: Use disease-free certified seed (pathogen-tested). Hot water seed treatment (50°C for 25 min). Use disease-free transplants. Drip irrigation. Crop rotation.
tomato_bacterial_spot.cultural_management: Avoid working in fields when plants are wet. Remove infected plant material.
tomato_bacterial_spot.sanitation: Destroy infected crop debris. Do not save seed from infected crops.
tomato_bacterial_spot.water_irrigation_management: Drip irrigation preferred. Avoid overhead irrigation.
tomato_bacterial_spot.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2–3 years.
tomato_bacterial_spot.resistant_varieties: Some tolerant varieties available. Consult ICAR-IIVR or state agricultural universities.
tomato_bacterial_spot.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE for commercial use in reviewed Indian sources.
tomato_bacterial_spot.chemical_control: Use only products registered/labeled for tomato bacterial spot in your region. Copper-based bactericides commonly used — consult local extension.
tomato_bacterial_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: Rapid defoliation or widespread fruit spotting warrants expert consultation.

tomato_early_blight.scientific_name: Alternaria solani (Ellis & G. Martin) L.R. Jones & Grout; also Alternaria tomatophila E.G. Simmons
tomato_early_blight.leaf_symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions with CONCENTRIC RINGS forming a target-board ('bull's-eye') pattern. Lesions have prominent yellow CHLOROTIC HALOS. OLDER/LOWER leaves affected first. Lesions typically 0.5–2 cm.
tomato_early_blight.stem_symptoms: Dark elongated lesions on stems near soil level (collar rot) and at petiole attachment.
tomato_early_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery, target-patterned lesions at stem end or on other parts of fruit. Fruit lesions have concentric rings and may have velvety dark sporulation.
tomato_early_blight.early_symptoms: Small (2–4 mm) dark spots on oldest/lowest leaves.
tomato_early_blight.advanced_symptoms: Large target-patterned necrotic lesions with yellow halos. Premature defoliation from lower canopy upward.
tomato_early_blight.visual_appearance: Circular dark brown lesions with concentric rings and yellow chlorotic halos, predominantly on older lower leaves.
tomato_early_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: CONCENTRIC RING/TARGET pattern within dark brown lesion on OLDER leaves — classic for Alternaria early blight.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_late_blight (rapidly expanding, no concentric rings, white sporulation on underside)
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot (smaller, circular, white center with tiny pycnidia)
tomato_target_spot (Corynespora — similar but may have more distinct yellow halo and sporulation)
tomato_early_blight.visual_differentiation: Early Blight: concentric rings, yellow halo, older leaves. Late Blight: rapidly expanding water-soaked dark lesion, white sporulation underside, affects younger/upper leaves. Septoria: tiny circular spots with white centers and dark pycnidia.
tomato_early_blight.disease_cycle_summary: Alternaria solani survives in crop residue and contaminated seed. Conidia dispersed by wind and rain splash. Multiple infection cycles occur. Plants under nutrient stress or physiological senescence are more susceptible.
tomato_early_blight.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash of conidia.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (24–29°C) are most favorable. Unlike Late Blight, Early Blight prefers warmer conditions.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness (>2–3 hours) facilitate infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Alternating wet and dry weather can accelerate disease cycles. Rain splash disperses conidia.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: Low nitrogen or potassium increases plant susceptibility. Older senescing tissue is more susceptible.

tomato_early_blight.growth_stage_context: Most damaging from flowering onwards as lower leaves begin to senesce. Premature defoliation affects fruit set and quality.
tomato_early_blight.monitoring_guidance: Scout from transplanting. Focus on older lower leaves. Record % incidence and severity.
tomato_early_blight.prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds (treated). Practice crop rotation (2–3 years) with non-solanaceous crops. Remove infected lower leaves. Maintain balanced plant nutrition (avoid N and K deficiency). Proper plant spacing.
tomato_early_blight.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris. Stake plants for good airflow. Avoid water stress.
tomato_early_blight.sanitation: Remove and destroy crop residue. Deep ploughing.
tomato_early_blight.water_irrigation_management: Drip irrigation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Irrigate in the morning.
tomato_early_blight.crop_rotation: Rotate with cereals or legumes for 2–3 years.
tomato_early_blight.resistant_varieties: Some partially resistant varieties available. Consult ICAR-IIVR for current recommendations.
tomato_early_blight.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE for commercial use from reviewed Indian sources.
tomato_early_blight.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for tomato early blight in your region. Consult local extension for registered fungicide options and spray schedule.
tomato_early_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: Severe defoliation before fruiting stage warrants expert consultation.

tomato_healthy.leaf_symptoms: Compound pinnate leaves, deep green, no lesions, no mottling, no curling.
tomato_healthy.visual_appearance: Deep green compound leaves with no visible spots, lesions, or discoloration.
tomato_healthy.visual_differentiation: Healthy tomato leaves show no spots, no yellowing from tip/margin, no curling, and no mottling.
tomato_healthy.monitoring_guidance: Scout weekly. Monitor older leaves for early blight. Check undersides for late blight sporulation after cool humid nights. Monitor for TYLCV curl symptoms and whiteflies.
tomato_healthy.prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants. Practice crop rotation. Maintain balanced nutrition. Control whitefly and other sucking pests.
tomato_healthy.cultural_management: Maintain field hygiene. Stake plants for airflow.
tomato_healthy.sanitation: Remove and destroy infected crop debris after harvest.
tomato_healthy.water_irrigation_management: Drip irrigation preferred. Avoid overhead irrigation.
tomato_healthy.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2–3 years.
tomato_healthy.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE for general advice — consult ICAR-IIVR.

tomato_late_blight.leaf_symptoms: Irregular dark brown-black water-soaked lesions, often starting from leaf margins, expanding rapidly. White cottony sporulation (sporangiophores) visible on the UNDERSIDE of lesions under humid conditions. Lesions appear greasy and water-soaked initially. Entire leaves may be killed within days under epidemic conditions.
tomato_late_blight.stem_symptoms: Dark brown-black elongated lesions on stems. Stems may be girdled causing collapse.
tomato_late_blight.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Greenish-brown water-soaked lesions on fruit, becoming brown, firm, and greasy. White sporulation visible in humid conditions on fruit lesions.
tomato_late_blight.early_symptoms: Pale to dark green water-soaked spots at leaf margins or tips.
tomato_late_blight.advanced_symptoms: Rapidly expanding dark brown-black lesions with white sporulation on underside. Rapid defoliation and plant collapse.
tomato_late_blight.visual_appearance: Dark brown-black irregular lesions, rapidly expanding, with white cottony sporulation on leaf undersides in humid conditions.
tomato_late_blight.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Rapidly expanding dark water-soaked lesions + WHITE COTTONY SPORULATION on leaf underside — pathognomonic for late blight.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_early_blight (slower, concentric rings, older leaves, no white sporulation)
tomato_late_blight.visual_differentiation: Late Blight: rapid dark water-soaked expansion, white underside sporulation in humidity. Early Blight: concentric rings on older leaves, slower progression.
tomato_late_blight.disease_cycle_summary: P. infestans survives in infected tomato/potato volunteers. Sporangia wind-dispersed; infection in cool humid conditions. Can destroy field in 7–10 days under epidemic conditions.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Cool temperatures (10–20°C) are optimal. Disease arrested at temperatures above 30°C.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High relative humidity (>90%) for 10–12+ hours required for sporulation and infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Prolonged cool, wet, humid nights and days drive rapid epidemics.

tomato_late_blight.growth_stage_context: All stages susceptible. Fruiting stage infection causes most economic damage through fruit rot.
tomato_late_blight.monitoring_guidance: Scout DAILY during cool humid weather. Check leaf undersides for white sporulation. Alert for geographic spread from potato fields.
tomato_late_blight.prevention: Avoid planting tomato near potato. Use certified disease-free transplants. Resistant varieties. Preventive fungicide application in late blight-endemic areas before symptoms appear.
tomato_late_blight.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected plant material IMMEDIATELY. Do not compost infected material.
tomato_late_blight.sanitation: Destroy infected plants. Remove volunteer tomato/potato plants in field and surrounding area.
tomato_late_blight.water_irrigation_management: Drip irrigation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Do not irrigate in evening under cool humid conditions.
tomato_late_blight.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops. Avoid tomato after potato in same field.
tomato_late_blight.resistant_varieties: Late blight resistant tomato varieties available. Consult ICAR-IIVR for current recommendations.
tomato_late_blight.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE for commercial practical use from reviewed Indian sources.
tomato_late_blight.chemical_control: Use only products registered/labeled for tomato late blight in your region. Preventive application is essential — consult ICAR-IIVR or local extension for registered options.
tomato_late_blight.expert_escalation_conditions: IMMEDIATE expert consultation required on confirmed late blight. Emergency spray intervention critical.

tomato_leaf_mold.scientific_name: Passalora fulva (Cooke) U. Braun & Crous (formerly Fulvia fulva; Cladosporium fulvum)
tomato_leaf_mold.leaf_symptoms: Pale green to yellow diffuse spots on UPPER leaf surface corresponding to characteristic OLIVE-GREEN to BROWNISH VELVETY SPORULATION (conidia masses) on the LOWER leaf surface. Spots are not sharply defined on upper surface. Lower surface sporulation is the most distinctive feature.
tomato_leaf_mold.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Occasionally infects blossoms and fruits, causing dark greenish-brown sporulation on fruit.
tomato_leaf_mold.early_symptoms: Pale green-yellow patches on upper leaf surface.
tomato_leaf_mold.advanced_symptoms: Extensive pale yellow upper leaf blotches with dense olive-green velvet sporulation on undersides. Severely affected leaves may wither.
tomato_leaf_mold.visual_appearance: Olive-green to brownish velvety sporulation on leaf undersides; corresponding pale yellow patches on upper surface.
tomato_leaf_mold.distinctive_symptom_pattern: VELVETY OLIVE-GREEN/BROWN SPORULATION on LEAF UNDERSIDE with corresponding pale yellow patches on upper surface — highly distinctive.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_late_blight (white sporulation, rapidly expanding dark lesions)
Downy mildew of other crops (not tomato — different pathogen)
tomato_leaf_mold.visual_differentiation: Leaf mold: olive-green velvety underside sporulation, pale upper patches. Late Blight: white sporulation on underside, dark rapidly-expanding lesions.
tomato_leaf_mold.disease_cycle_summary: Fungus survives as conidia and stromata in plant debris and infected seed. Disease thrives in protected cultivation (greenhouses, polyhouses) and in humid outdoor conditions. Conidia wind-dispersed.
tomato_leaf_mold.spread_mechanism: Wind and air currents dispersing conidia within crops. Most severe in protected cultivation environments.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Moderate temperatures (20–25°C) are optimal for leaf mold development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: Very high relative humidity (>85%) is required. Disease is particularly severe in protected cultivation where humidity remains high.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Free moisture not required — high relative humidity alone is sufficient for spore germination. Most severe in humid growing environments.

tomato_leaf_mold.growth_stage_context: Can occur at any stage, but often more severe as crop matures and canopy becomes dense. Worse in protected cultivation.
tomato_leaf_mold.monitoring_guidance: Inspect UNDERSIDE of leaves weekly. Monitor humidity in protected structures. Ensure adequate ventilation in polyhouses.
tomato_leaf_mold.prevention: Maintain relative humidity below 85% in protected structures through ventilation. Increase air circulation in open field through proper plant spacing. Remove infected leaves. Use resistant varieties.
tomato_leaf_mold.cultural_management: Remove infected leaves promptly. Prune for better airflow. Ventilate protected structures.
tomato_leaf_mold.sanitation: Remove and destroy infected plant material. Clean greenhouse between crops.
tomato_leaf_mold.water_irrigation_management: Drip irrigation. Avoid overhead systems that raise humidity.
tomato_leaf_mold.crop_rotation: Relevant in greenhouse — rotate or sterilize growing medium.
tomato_leaf_mold.resistant_varieties: Several Cf resistance gene-based resistant tomato varieties are commercially available. Consult seed companies or ICAR-IIVR for current resistant variety recommendations.
tomato_leaf_mold.biological_control: NOT_AVAILABLE for commercial use in reviewed Indian extension sources.
tomato_leaf_mold.chemical_control: Use only products registered/labeled for tomato leaf mold in your region. Consult local extension for registered fungicide options.
tomato_leaf_mold.expert_escalation_conditions: Severe outbreak in protected cultivation warrants expert consultation on humidity management and fungicide resistance status.

tomato_mosaic_virus.scientific_name: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) — formerly grouped with Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV); now classified separately
tomato_mosaic_virus.pathogen_or_cause: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), a Tobamovirus. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) also infects tomato.
tomato_mosaic_virus.leaf_symptoms: Characteristic mosaic pattern — alternating light green, yellow, and dark green patches on leaf surface. Leaf distortion and curling may occur. Interveinal chlorosis, fern-leaf symptom (in severe cases leaf blades are greatly reduced). Mottling and blistering.
tomato_mosaic_virus.stem_symptoms: Necrotic streaks on stems in some strains.
tomato_mosaic_virus.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Internal browning of fruit, discoloration, and uneven ripening. 'Bronze' coloration of fruits in some strains.
tomato_mosaic_virus.early_symptoms: Young leaves show mosaic (mottled) green-yellow pattern and mild curling.
tomato_mosaic_virus.advanced_symptoms: Severe mosaic and distortion. Fern-leaf (severe leaf reduction). Stunting.
tomato_mosaic_virus.visual_appearance: Alternating light/dark green mottled (mosaic) pattern on leaves. Leaves may be distorted or fern-like.
tomato_mosaic_virus.distinctive_symptom_pattern: MOSAIC (alternating light/dark green patches) on leaves, combined with leaf distortion — characteristic of tobamovirus infection.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus (upward leaf curl with chlorosis, not true mosaic pattern)
tomato_mosaic_virus.visual_differentiation: Mosaic virus: alternating light/dark green mottling (mosaic) on leaves. TYLCV: upward leaf curl with yellowing and small leaves.
tomato_mosaic_virus.disease_cycle_summary: ToMV persists in soil and crop debris for extended periods. Transmitted mechanically through contact (workers, tools, mechanical handling). No insect vector. Also seed-transmitted. Very stable in the environment.
tomato_mosaic_virus.spread_mechanism: Mechanical transmission through contact (worker hands, tools, clothing, water). Also seed-borne. NOT insect-transmitted (no vector).

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Virus persists and spreads mechanically regardless of temperature. Symptom expression may be masked at high temperatures (>32°C).
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — disease is mechanically transmitted and not primarily driven by humidity.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: NOT_AVAILABLE.
favorable_environmental_conditions.soil_context: NOT_AVAILABLE — virus can persist in soil and plant debris.

tomato_mosaic_virus.growth_stage_context: Infection at seedling or transplant stage causes most severe impact on yield.
tomato_mosaic_virus.monitoring_guidance: Inspect seedlings and transplants before purchase. Scout for mosaic patterns. Remove symptomatic plants early.
tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Use certified ToMV/TMV-free seeds or treated seeds. Use resistant varieties (Tm gene resistance). Disinfect tools and hands with soap/water or disinfectant between plants. Do not handle plants after handling tobacco products (tobacco is a source of TMV). Raise nursery in protected area.
tomato_mosaic_virus.cultural_management: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Do not compost infected material. Wash hands thoroughly before handling tomato plants. Disinfect tools between rows.
tomato_mosaic_virus.sanitation: Destroy infected plant residue. Sterilize greenhouse growing media.
tomato_mosaic_virus.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops to reduce soil-borne inoculum.
tomato_mosaic_virus.resistant_varieties: Varieties with Tm-2a gene resistance to ToMV are commercially available. Consult ICAR-IIVR or seed companies for currently available resistant varieties.
tomato_mosaic_virus.chemical_control: No chemical treatment available for viral diseases. Chemical management is NOT applicable for this disease.
tomato_mosaic_virus.expert_escalation_conditions: If infection rate in nursery exceeds 5–10%, replace entire seedling batch with certified disease-free plants.

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.leaf_symptoms: Numerous SMALL (1.5–4 mm) circular spots with WHITE to GRAY CENTERS and DARK BROWN borders. TINY DARK PYCNIDIA (fungal fruiting bodies) visible in the center of lesions (visible to naked eye or with hand lens). Yellow halo may be present. Lower/older leaves affected first.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.stem_symptoms: Dark lesions on stems possible. Calyx lesions possible.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Fruit not commonly affected but calyx infection can occur.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.early_symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on lower leaves.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.advanced_symptoms: Numerous small spots on all lower-canopy leaves, causing mass yellowing and premature defoliation.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.visual_appearance: Many small circular spots with white-gray centers and dark borders; tiny dark dots (pycnidia) visible in lesion center.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: MANY SMALL CIRCULAR SPOTS with WHITE/GRAY CENTERS, DARK BORDERS, and TINY PYCNIDIA in center — highly distinctive for Septoria.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_early_blight (larger, concentric ring lesions, no pycnidia)
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.visual_differentiation: Septoria: MANY SMALL spots with WHITE centers and visible PYCNIDIA. Early Blight: LARGER spots with CONCENTRIC RINGS, no pycnidia. Bacterial spot: angular lesions with yellow halo, no pycnidia.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.disease_cycle_summary: S. lycopersici survives in infected crop debris and seed. Conidia from pycnidia are released during rain and splash to lower leaves. Multiple infection cycles per season.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.spread_mechanism: Rain splash of conidia from pycnidia; infected crop debris.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Cool to moderate temperatures (20–25°C) favor disease development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness (>3 hours) required for infection.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Frequent rain splash is critical for conidia dispersal from pycnidia. Disease severe in wet growing seasons.

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.growth_stage_context: Disease commonly appears from transplanting onwards on lower leaves. Particularly severe when lower canopy is moist.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.monitoring_guidance: Scout lower canopy leaves from transplanting. Use hand lens to confirm pycnidia presence.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Crop rotation (2–3 years) with non-solanaceous crops. Remove infected lower leaves. Proper plant spacing. Use disease-free seed. Stake plants for better airflow.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.cultural_management: Remove infected lower leaves. Stake plants. Avoid working in wet fields.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.sanitation: Destroy infected plant debris. Deep ploughing.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.crop_rotation: Essential — rotate 2–3 years with non-solanaceous crops.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE — no commercially resistant variety widely documented in reviewed Indian sources.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.chemical_control: Use only products registered/labeled for Septoria leaf spot of tomato in your region. Consult local extension for registered fungicide options.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: Severe early defoliation before fruiting warrants expert consultation.

tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.pathogen_or_cause: Tetranychus urticae Koch (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) — an arachnid pest, not a fungus or virus
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.leaf_symptoms: Tiny yellow stippling (pinpoint chlorotic spots) on upper leaf surface caused by mite feeding. As infestation progresses, leaves develop a bronzed, dried, or dusty appearance. Fine webbing (silk strands) on leaf underside and between leaves at high mite densities. Tiny moving red/green dots visible on leaf underside.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.stem_symptoms: Fine webbing on stems at high infestation levels.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Silver-gray scarring or bronzing of fruit surface in heavy infestations.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.early_symptoms: Tiny yellow stipples on upper leaf surface (difficult to see without magnification). Slight bronzing.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.advanced_symptoms: Severe bronzing and drying of leaves. Dense white webbing on undersides. Defoliation in very severe cases.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.visual_appearance: Yellow stippled/bronzed upper leaf surface. Fine white webbing on leaf underside. Tiny red/green dots (mites) visible with magnification on leaf underside.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Fine WEBBING on leaf underside with YELLOW STIPPLING on upper surface and visible tiny moving MITES — characteristic of spider mite infestation.
lookalike_conditions: Drought stress (wilting, no webbing or stippling)
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.visual_differentiation: Spider mites: visible webbing + stippling + tiny mites visible on underside. Fungal/bacterial diseases: no webbing. Drought: general wilting, no stippling or webbing.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.disease_cycle_summary: Tetranychus urticae overwinters as adult females. Under hot dry conditions, mite populations can double every 5–7 days. Each female lays 100+ eggs. Multiple generations per season. Natural enemies (predatory mites, lacewings) provide significant biological control when not disrupted by pesticides.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.spread_mechanism: Wind, workers, equipment, and plant-to-plant contact spread mites. Incoming infected transplants or plant material.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Hot, dry conditions (27–35°C) favor rapid population explosion. Development arrested at high humidity.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: LOW humidity (<50%) strongly favors mite population growth. High humidity (>80%) slows mite development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Dry conditions favor mite outbreaks. Rain and misting suppress mite populations mechanically.

tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.growth_stage_context: Can occur at any stage. Most damaging at flowering and fruit development. Hot dry periods during summer crops are high-risk.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.monitoring_guidance: Use 10X hand lens to inspect underside of leaves at regular intervals. Count mites per leaf. Economic threshold varies — consult local extension guidance.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.prevention: Monitor regularly, particularly during hot dry periods. Maintain field hygiene. Avoid broad-spectrum pesticides that kill natural enemies (predatory mites). Use reflective mulches to deter mite colonization. Maintain adequate plant moisture (drought stress increases susceptibility).
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.cultural_management: Use water sprays to knock mites off plants during early infestation. Avoid dusty field conditions. Remove heavily infested plant parts.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.sanitation: Remove and destroy heavily infested plant debris. Remove volunteer tomato plants.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.water_irrigation_management: Maintain adequate soil moisture. Drip irrigation. Overhead irrigation can physically dislodge mites — balance against disease risk.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.resistant_varieties: NOT_AVAILABLE from reviewed sources for commercial tomato spider mite resistance.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.biological_control: Predatory mites (Phytoseiidae family: Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus) are effective biological control agents in both protected and open field cultivation. Encourage natural predators by avoiding broad-spectrum pesticides.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.chemical_control: Use only products currently registered/labeled for two-spotted spider mite on tomato in your region. Rotate miticide classes to prevent resistance development. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators. Consult local extension for registered miticide options.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.expert_escalation_conditions: Rapid population explosion or miticide failure (resistance) warrants expert consultation. If webbing covers >25% of plant canopy, urgent management is needed.
tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.knowledge_notes: This is a pest/arthropod infestation — NOT a fungal, bacterial, or viral disease. Chemical control uses miticides, not fungicides.

tomato_target_spot.scientific_name: Corynespora cassiicola (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) C.T. Wei
tomato_target_spot.leaf_symptoms: Dark brown lesions (5–20 mm) with visible CONCENTRIC RINGS (target pattern) but typically larger than early blight lesions and with a more prominent yellow halo. Lesions may appear anywhere on leaves (not restricted to older leaves as strongly as early blight). Small water-soaked spots progressing to dark brown.
tomato_target_spot.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Dark, slightly sunken lesions on fruit.
tomato_target_spot.early_symptoms: Small (2–5 mm) dark brown spots on leaves.
tomato_target_spot.advanced_symptoms: Larger target-pattern lesions with yellow halos. Defoliation.
tomato_target_spot.visual_appearance: Dark brown to black circular lesions with concentric banding and yellow halos, similar to early blight but often larger and with more diffuse pattern.
tomato_target_spot.distinctive_symptom_pattern: Target/concentric-ring pattern, but generally larger and less strictly on older leaves compared to early blight. Occurs in warm humid conditions.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_early_blight (smaller lesions, strictly on older leaves, same concentric ring pattern)
tomato_late_blight (no rings, rapidly expanding, white sporulation)
tomato_target_spot.visual_differentiation: Target spot: large concentric ring lesions, can affect all leaf ages. Early blight: similar but strictly on older/lower leaves, smaller. These two are most commonly confused.
tomato_target_spot.disease_cycle_summary: C. cassiicola survives in plant debris and infected seed. Spores are wind and rain splash dispersed. Disease favored by warm humid conditions. Wide host range.
tomato_target_spot.spread_mechanism: Wind and rain splash dispersal of conidia.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm conditions (24–32°C) favor disease development.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Warm, wet conditions accelerate development.

tomato_target_spot.growth_stage_context: More commonly seen from flowering stage onwards.
tomato_target_spot.monitoring_guidance: Inspect all leaf canopy levels. Cannot distinguish reliably from early blight without laboratory confirmation.
tomato_target_spot.prevention: Same practices as for early blight: crop rotation, certified seed, plant spacing, drip irrigation.
tomato_target_spot.cultural_management: Remove infected leaves. Improve canopy airflow.
tomato_target_spot.chemical_control: Use only products registered/labeled for this disease on tomato in your region. Consult local extension.
tomato_target_spot.expert_escalation_conditions: Severe defoliation warrants expert consultation. Laboratory confirmation recommended to distinguish from early blight.
tomato_target_spot.knowledge_notes: Target spot and early blight are frequently confused. Laboratory confirmation (microscopy/PCR) recommended for definitive diagnosis.

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.scientific_name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) — a monopartite Begomovirus
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.pathogen_or_cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci (Genn.)
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.leaf_symptoms: Characteristic UPWARD CURLING and CUPPING of young leaves with YELLOWING of leaf margins and interveinal areas. Leaves are small, crinkled, and cupped (inward curling). The yellowing and curl are most pronounced on young/newly emerging leaves.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.stem_symptoms: Shortened internodes. Upright ('erect') growth habit. Stunted plant.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.fruit_pod_tuber_symptoms: Fewer fruits. Fruits may be smaller. Fruit set drastically reduced in early-infected plants.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.early_symptoms: Young leaves show yellowing of margins and interveinal areas with slight upward curling.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.advanced_symptoms: Severe leaf curl with pronounced cupping. All young leaves are yellow-margined and curled. Stunted plant with bushy appearance due to shortened internodes. Near-total yield loss if infected before flowering.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.visual_appearance: Young leaves curled upward with prominent yellowing at margins and between veins. Small, deformed, cupped leaves on stunted plant.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.distinctive_symptom_pattern: UPWARD CUPPING of young leaves with YELLOW MARGINS and interveinal chlorosis, combined with plant STUNTING — pathognomonic for TYLCV. Compare: tomato mosaic virus shows mosaic on older leaves without upward cup-curl.
lookalike_conditions: tomato_mosaic_virus (mosaic pattern on leaves — not the same as cup-curl with yellowing)
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.visual_differentiation: TYLCV: young leaves cup-curled upward with yellow margins and interveinal chlorosis. Mosaic virus: mottled/mosaic pattern on leaves without pronounced cup-curl. TYLCV affects young leaves; mosaic typically affects older leaves first.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.disease_cycle_summary: TYLCV is transmitted exclusively by whitefly Bemisia tabaci in a persistent circulative manner. The virus cannot be transmitted mechanically or by seed. Whitefly acquires the virus in as little as 15–30 minutes of feeding and transmits it for its lifetime.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.spread_mechanism: Exclusively by whitefly Bemisia tabaci — persistent, circulative, non-propagative transmission. Whitefly can transmit for its entire lifespan after a brief acquisition access period.

favorable_environmental_conditions.temperature_context: Warm temperatures (27–35°C) favor whitefly population growth and rapid TYLCV spread.
favorable_environmental_conditions.humidity_context: Low-moderate humidity favors whitefly multiplication and TYLCV spread.
favorable_environmental_conditions.rainfall_wetness_context: Hot, dry periods coincide with high whitefly populations and TYLCV epidemics.

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.growth_stage_context: Seedling and early vegetative stages are most vulnerable. Plants infected before flowering suffer near-complete yield loss. Infections after fruit set are less damaging.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.monitoring_guidance: Monitor whitefly populations using yellow sticky traps (2 per acre) from seedling stage. Inspect growing tips for curl symptoms weekly. Scout border rows first.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.prevention: Use certified TYLCV-free, virus-tested transplants. Raise nursery under 50-mesh nylon insect-proof net. Use TYLCV-resistant varieties (primary management strategy). Remove and destroy TYLCV-infected plants immediately. Remove alternate host weeds (Solanum nigrum, Datura, etc.). Avoid tomato planting near cucurbit or other whitefly host crops.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.cultural_management: Rogue out infected plants early. Remove weed hosts in and around field. Use reflective mulches (silver) to reduce whitefly landing.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.sanitation: Remove infected crop debris. Remove volunteer tomato plants. Destroy alternate host weeds.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.water_irrigation_management: Maintain plant vigor. Avoid water stress which may increase plant susceptibility.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.crop_rotation: Avoid continuous tomato. Rotate with cereals/legumes.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.resistant_varieties: TYLCV-resistant tomato varieties are commercially available in India and are the primary management strategy. Consult ICAR-IIVR, state KVK, or seed companies for current resistant variety recommendations for your region.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.biological_control: Encourage Encarsia formosa and other whitefly parasitoids. Neem-based products used as part of IPM for whitefly management — consult product label and local extension.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.chemical_control: No chemical treatment is effective against the virus. Whitefly vector control reduces spread. Use only products currently registered/labeled for whitefly control on tomato in your region. Consult local agricultural extension for registered insecticide options and rates for vector management. Avoid overusing any single class to prevent resistance.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.expert_escalation_conditions: If >20% of plants are infected before flowering, contact extension officer. Consider crop destruction and replanting with resistant variety if infection is widespread before fruit set.
